sentences.zh: 25%唐有鹽池十八，井六百四十，皆隸度支。

translations.literal: The Tang had eighteen salt ponds and six hundred forty wells, all subordinate to the Department of Revenue.
translations.idiomatic: Under the Tang there were eighteen salt ponds and six hundred forty salt wells, all administered by the Department of Revenue.

sentences.zh: 蒲州安邑、解縣有池五，總曰「兩池」，歲得鹽萬斛，以供京師。

translations.literal: In Anyi and Jie counties of Puzhou there were five ponds, collectively called the "Two Pools," yielding ten thousand hu of salt yearly to supply the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Puzhou's Anyi and Jie counties had five ponds, known together as the "Two Pools," which produced ten thousand hu of salt each year for the capital.

sentences.zh: 鹽州五原有烏池、白池、瓦池、細項池，靈州有溫泉池、兩井池、長尾池、五泉池、紅桃池、回樂池、弘靜池、會州有河池，三州皆輸米以代鹽。

translations.literal: Wuyuan in Yanzhou had the Wuchi, Baichi, Wachi, and Xixiang ponds; Lingzhou had the Wenquan, Liangjing, Changwei, Wuquan, Hongtao, Huile, and Hongjing ponds; Huizhou had the Hechi pond; the three prefectures all submitted grain in lieu of salt.
translations.idiomatic: At Wuyuan in Yan Prefecture were the Black, White, Tile, and Fine-Item ponds; Ling Prefecture had the Hot Spring, Two Wells, Long Tail, Five Springs, Red Peach, Huile, and Hongjing ponds; and Huiz Prefecture had the River Pond—all three prefectures paid grain taxes in place of salt tribute.

sentences.zh: 安北都護府有胡落池，歲得鹽萬四千斛，以給振武、天德。

translations.literal: The Anbei Protectorate had the Huluo pond, yielding fourteen thousand hu of salt yearly, to supply Zhenwu and Tiande.
translations.idiomatic: The Anbei Protectorate's Huluo Pond yielded fourteen thousand hu of salt a year, earmarked for the Zhenwu and Tiande garrisons.

sentences.zh: 黔州有井四十一，成州、巂州井各一，果、閬、開、通井百二十三，山南西院領之。

translations.literal: Qianzhou had forty-one wells; Chengzhou and Xizhou each had one; Guo, Lang, Kai, and Tong had one hundred twenty-three wells altogether, administered by the Southwestern Shannan Circuit.
translations.idiomatic: Qian Prefecture had forty-one wells; Cheng and Xi each had one; and Guo, Lang, Kai, and Tong together had one hundred twenty-three—all overseen by the Southwestern Shannan salt office.

sentences.zh: 邛、眉、嘉有井十三，劍南西川院領之。

translations.literal: Qiong, Mei, and Jia had thirteen wells, administered by the Western Sichuan Circuit office.
translations.idiomatic: Qiong, Mei, and Jia prefectures maintained thirteen wells under the Western Sichuan salt office.

sentences.zh: 梓、遂、緜、合、昌、渝、瀘、資、榮、陵、簡有井四百六十，劍南東川院領之。

translations.literal: Zi, Sui, Mian, He, Chang, Yu, Lu, Zi, Rong, Ling, and Jian had four hundred sixty wells, administered by the Eastern Sichuan Circuit office.
translations.idiomatic: Zi, Sui, Mian, He, Chang, Yu, Lu, Zi, Rong, Ling, and Jian had four hundred sixty wells combined, all under the Eastern Sichuan salt office.

sentences.zh: 皆隨月督課。

translations.literal: All were supervised for monthly quotas.
translations.idiomatic: Each site was monitored month by month for production quotas.

sentences.zh: 幽州、大同橫野軍有鹽屯，每屯有丁有兵，歲得鹽二千八百斛，下者千五百斛。

translations.literal: Youzhou and Datong Hengye Army had salt colonies; each colony had laborers and troops, yielding twenty-eight hundred hu yearly at best, fifteen hundred at least.
translations.idiomatic: You Prefecture and Datong's Hengye Army maintained salt farms; every farm had civilian laborers and soldiers, producing up to twenty-eight hundred hu a year and no less than fifteen hundred.

sentences.zh: 負海州歲免租為鹽二萬斛以輸司農。

translations.literal: Maritime prefectures were exempted from land tax yearly in exchange for twenty thousand hu of salt submitted to the Commissioner of Revenue.
translations.idiomatic: Coastal prefectures were excused from grain rents each year on condition that they delivered twenty thousand hu of salt to the Commissioner's office.

sentences.zh: 青、楚、海、滄、棣、杭、蘇等州，以鹽價市輕貨，亦輸司農。

translations.literal: Qing, Chu, Hai, Cang, Di, Hang, Su, and other prefectures used salt prices to purchase light goods, also submitting to the Commissioner of Revenue.
translations.idiomatic: Qing, Chu, Hai, Cang, Di, Hang, Su, and other prefectures converted salt revenues into lightweight goods for transport, likewise forwarding them to the Commissioner.

sentences.zh: 天寶、至德間，鹽每斗十錢。

translations.literal: Between the Tianbao and Zhide eras, salt was ten cash per dou.
translations.idiomatic: From the Tianbao through the Zhide reigns, salt sold for ten cash per dou.

sentences.zh: 乾元元年，鹽鐵、鑄錢使第五琦初變鹽法，就山海井竈近利之地置監院，游民業鹽者為亭戶，免雜傜。

translations.literal: In the first year of Qianyuan, the Salt, Iron, and Coinage Commissioner Diwu Qi first changed the salt law: he established supervisory offices in places near mountains, seas, wells, and saltworks where profit was easy; vagrants who worked in salt became "pavilion households," exempt from miscellaneous corvée.
translations.idiomatic: In 758, Salt and Iron Commissioner Diwu Qi overhauled the salt law: he placed inspectorates wherever mountains, seas, wells, or brine furnaces offered easy profit; itinerant laborers who took up salt-making were registered as pavilion households and freed from miscellaneous corvée.

sentences.zh: 盜鬻者論以法。

translations.literal: Those who stole and sold illegally were punished according to law.
translations.idiomatic: Illegal salt trading was prosecuted under the full force of the law.

sentences.zh: 及琦為諸州榷鹽鐵使，盡榷天下鹽，斗加時價百錢而出之，為錢一百一十。

translations.literal: When Qi became Commissioner for Salt and Iron Monopoly in all prefectures, he monopolized all salt under heaven; each dou had one hundred cash added to the market price when sold, making one hundred ten cash.
translations.idiomatic: Once Qi became national salt-and-iron monopolist, he brought all salt under state control, adding one hundred cash to the market price per dou and selling it for one hundred ten cash.

sentences.zh: 自兵起，流庸未復，稅賦不足供費，鹽鐵使劉晏以為因民所急而稅之，則國足用。

translations.literal: Since the rebellion began, displaced persons had not returned, and tax revenues were insufficient for expenses; the Salt and Iron Commissioner Liu Yan held that by taxing what the people urgently needed, the state would have enough.
translations.idiomatic: After the rebellion erupted, refugees had still not returned home and ordinary taxes could not cover expenses. Salt Commissioner Liu Yan argued that if the state taxed what people could not do without, the treasury would be adequately supplied.

sentences.zh: 於是上鹽法輕重之宜，以鹽吏多則州縣擾，出鹽鄉因舊監置吏，亭戶糶商人，縱其所之。

translations.literal: Thereupon he submitted on the proper balance of light and heavy in the salt law: since many salt officials meant harassment of prefectures and counties, in salt-producing districts he placed officials according to old supervisory posts; pavilion households sold to merchants, who were allowed to transport wherever they wished.
translations.idiomatic: Accordingly he memorialized on the proper balance of the salt levies: too many salt officials meant trouble for local government, so in producing districts he kept the old inspectorates; pavilion households sold to merchants, who could ship salt wherever demand lay.

sentences.zh: 江、嶺去鹽遠者，有常平鹽，每商人不至，則減價以糶民，官收厚利而人不知貴。

translations.literal: In Jiang and Ling regions far from salt, there was "ever-normal" salt; whenever merchants did not arrive, prices were lowered to sell to the people—the government collected thick profits while the people did not know it was expensive.
translations.idiomatic: In the Yangzi basin and Lingnan, far from producing areas, the state maintained ever-normal salt reserves; when merchants failed to arrive, prices were cut to sell to common people—the treasury still took a heavy profit while the public scarcely felt the burden.

sentences.zh: 晏又以鹽生霖潦則鹵薄，暵旱則土溜墳，乃隨時為令，遣吏曉導，倍於勸農。

translations.literal: Yan also held that when rains and floods came, brine grew thin; when drought came, soil washed away—thus he issued timely orders and sent officials to instruct and guide, doubling the effort of encouraging agriculture.
translations.idiomatic: Yan also knew that heavy rains diluted the brine and drought washed away the soil, so he issued seasonal orders and sent officials to instruct producers—devoting twice the zeal he would have shown in promoting agriculture.

sentences.zh: 吳、越、揚、楚鹽廩至數千，積鹽二萬餘石。

translations.literal: Wu, Yue, Yang, and Chu salt granaries numbered in the thousands, accumulating more than twenty thousand shi of salt.
translations.idiomatic: The Wu, Yue, Yang, and Chu circuits maintained thousands of salt storehouses holding more than twenty thousand shi of salt.

sentences.zh: 有漣水、湖州、越州、杭州四場，嘉興、海陵、鹽城、新亭、臨平、蘭亭、永嘉、大昌、候官、富都十監，歲得錢百餘萬緡，以當百餘州之賦。

translations.literal: There were the Lianshui, Huzhou, Yuezhou, and Hangzhou fields; the Jiaxing, Hailing, Yancheng, Xinting, Linping, Lanting, Yongjia, Dachang, Houguan, and Fudu offices; yearly revenue exceeded one million strings of cash, equivalent to the tax yield of more than one hundred prefectures.
translations.idiomatic: Four production fields—Lianshui, Huzhou, Yuezhou, and Hangzhou—and ten salt offices—Jiaxing, Hailing, Yancheng, Xinting, Linping, Lanting, Yongjia, Dachang, Houguan, and Fudu—together yielded more than a million strings of cash annually, equal to the tax revenue of over a hundred prefectures.

sentences.zh: 自淮北置巡院十三，曰揚州、陳許、汴州、廬壽、白沙、淮西、甬橋、浙西、宋州、泗州、嶺南、兗鄆、鄭滑，捕私鹽者，姦盜為之衰息。

translations.literal: From north of the Huai thirteen inspection posts were established—Yangzhou, Chenxu, Bianzhou, Lushou, Baisha, Huaixi, Yongqiao, Zhexi, Songzhou, Sizhou, Lingnan, Yanzhou-Yunzhou, and Zhengzhou-Hua Prefecture—to capture illegal salt traders; illicit smuggling accordingly declined.
translations.idiomatic: North of the Huai, thirteen patrol stations—from Yangzhou to Zhengzhou-Hua Prefecture—were established to hunt smugglers, and illegal traffic accordingly subsided.

sentences.zh: 然諸道加榷鹽錢，商人舟所過有稅。

translations.literal: Yet the various circuits added salt monopoly surcharges, and wherever merchants' boats passed there were taxes.
translations.idiomatic: Even so, regional circuits piled on salt surcharges, taxing merchant vessels at every stop along the waterways.

sentences.zh: 晏奏罷州縣率稅，禁堰埭邀以利者。

translations.literal: Yan memorialized to abolish prefecture and county assessment taxes and to forbid dam-and-ferry tolls levied for private profit.
translations.idiomatic: Yan petitioned to end ad hoc local surcharges and to outlaw dams and ferry barriers erected purely for extortion.

sentences.zh: 晏之始至也，鹽利歲纔四十萬緡，至大曆末，六百餘萬緡。

translations.literal: When Yan first arrived, salt profits were only four hundred thousand strings yearly; by the end of the Dali era, over six million strings.
translations.idiomatic: When Yan took office, annual salt revenues barely reached four hundred thousand strings; by the close of the Dali reign they exceeded six million.

sentences.zh: 天下之賦，鹽利居半，宮闈服御、軍饟、百官祿俸皆仰給焉。

translations.literal: Of all taxes under heaven, salt profits made up half; palace apparel, military provisions, and officials' salaries all depended on them.
translations.idiomatic: Salt revenues accounted for half the empire's tax intake; the palace wardrobe, army rations, and official salaries all depended on them.

sentences.zh: 明年而晏罷。

translations.literal: The next year Yan was dismissed.
translations.idiomatic: The following year Yan was removed from office.

sentences.zh: 貞元四年，淮南節度使陳少游奏加民賦，自此江淮鹽每斗亦增二百，為錢三百一十，其後復增六十，河中兩池鹽每斗為錢三百七十。

translations.literal: In the fourth year of Zhenyuan, Huainan Military Governor Chen Shaoyou memorialized to increase the people's tax levy; from this the Jiang-Huai salt price per dou also rose two hundred cash, reaching three hundred ten; later it rose another sixty; salt from the Two Pools in Hezhong reached three hundred seventy cash per dou.
translations.idiomatic: In 788, Huainan governor Chen Shaoyou won approval to raise civilian levies, and Jiang-Huai salt jumped two hundred cash per dou to three hundred ten; later it rose another sixty, while the Two Pools salt in Hezhong sold for three hundred seventy per dou.

sentences.zh: 江淮豪賈射利，或時倍之，官收不能過半，民始怨矣。

translations.literal: Powerful Jiang-Huai merchants seized profits, sometimes doubling prices; the government collected no more than half, and the people began to complain.
translations.idiomatic: Wealthy Jiang-Huai merchants hoarded profits, sometimes doubling the price; the state collected less than half the proceeds, and popular resentment began to stir.

sentences.zh: 劉晏鹽法既成，商人納絹以代鹽利者，每緡加錢二百，以備將士春服。

translations.literal: After Liu Yan's salt law was established, merchants who paid silk in lieu of salt profits had two hundred cash added per string, to provision soldiers' spring uniforms.
translations.idiomatic: Once Liu Yan's system was in place, merchants paying silk in lieu of salt dues paid an extra two hundred cash per string to fund soldiers' spring uniforms.

sentences.zh: 包佶為汴東水陸運、兩稅、鹽鐵使，許以漆器、瑇瑁、綾綺代鹽價，雖不可用者亦高估而售之，廣虛數以罔上。

translations.literal: Bao Ji served as Commissioner for Bian East Water-Land Transport, Two-Tax, and Salt-Iron; he permitted lacquerware, tortoise shell, and silk brocades to substitute for salt prices—even unusable goods were overvalued and sold, greatly inflating figures to deceive the throne.
translations.idiomatic: Commissioner Bao Ji allowed merchants to pay salt dues in lacquerware, tortoise shell, and brocades—even worthless goods were assigned inflated prices and accepted, swelling the reported totals to mislead the court.

sentences.zh: 亭戶冒法，私鬻不絕，巡捕之卒，遍于州縣。

translations.literal: Pavilion households violated the law, private sale never ceased, and patrol troops spread throughout prefectures and counties.
translations.idiomatic: Pavilion households broke the law and private sales never stopped; patrol troops fanned out through every prefecture and county.

sentences.zh: 鹽估益貴，商人乘時射利，遠鄉貧民困高估，至有淡食者。

translations.literal: Salt prices grew ever costlier; merchants seized profits in timely fashion; poor people in distant districts were distressed by overvaluation, to the point of eating without salt.
translations.idiomatic: Salt grew steadily dearer as merchants timed their profits; poor villagers in remote districts, crushed by inflated prices, sometimes went without salt altogether.

sentences.zh: 巡吏既多，官冗傷財，當時病之。

translations.literal: With many patrol officials, redundant bureaucracy wasted resources—this was the affliction of the time.
translations.idiomatic: The proliferation of patrol officers meant wasteful bureaucracy—a grievance widely noted at the time.

sentences.zh: 其後軍費日增，鹽價寖貴，有以穀數斗易鹽一升。

translations.literal: Later military expenses increased daily, salt prices gradually rose; some exchanged several dou of grain for one sheng of salt.
translations.idiomatic: As military costs mounted, salt prices kept climbing until several dou of grain might buy no more than a sheng of salt.

sentences.zh: 私糴犯法，未嘗少息。

translations.literal: Private purchase in violation of the law never ceased for a moment.
translations.idiomatic: Illicit private buying never slackened.

sentences.zh: 順宗時始減江淮鹽價，每斗為錢二百五十，河中兩池鹽，斗錢三百。

translations.literal: In Emperor Shunzong's time the Jiang-Huai salt price was first reduced to two hundred fifty cash per dou; the Two Pools salt in Hezhong was three hundred per dou.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Shunzong, Jiang-Huai salt was cut to two hundred fifty cash per dou and the Two Pools salt in Hezhong to three hundred.

sentences.zh: 增雲安、渙陽、塗𣉯三監。

translations.literal: Three offices were added—Yun'an, Huanyang, and Tujin.
translations.idiomatic: Three new salt offices were added at Yun'an, Huanyang, and Tujin.

sentences.zh: 其後鹽鐵使李錡奏江淮鹽斗減錢十以便民，未幾復舊。

translations.literal: Later Salt Commissioner Li Kai memorialized to reduce Jiang-Huai salt by ten cash per dou for the people's convenience; before long it was restored.
translations.idiomatic: Later Commissioner Li Kai proposed cutting Jiang-Huai salt by ten cash per dou to ease the burden on the people, but the reduction was soon withdrawn.

sentences.zh: 方是時，錡盛貢獻以固寵，朝廷大臣，皆餌以厚貨，鹽鐵之利，積于私室，而國用耗屈，榷鹽法大壞，多為虛估，率千錢不滿百三十而已。

translations.literal: At that time Kai made lavish tribute presentations to secure favor; court ministers were all fed rich gifts; salt and iron profits accumulated in private chambers while state funds were exhausted; the salt monopoly law was greatly damaged, with many inflated valuations—a thousand cash in goods worth barely one hundred thirty.
translations.idiomatic: Li Kai showered the throne with tribute to secure favor and bought off senior ministers with rich gifts; salt profits pooled in his private coffers while the treasury ran dry; the monopoly system collapsed into hollow valuations, so a thousand-cash assessment might yield barely one hundred thirty in real revenue.

sentences.zh: 兵部侍郎李巽為使，以鹽利皆歸度支，物無虛估，天下糶鹽稅茶，其贏六百六十五萬緡。

translations.literal: Vice Minister of War Li Xun became commissioner; salt profits all returned to the Department of Revenue, goods had no inflated valuation; selling salt and taxing tea under heaven yielded six million six hundred fifty thousand strings in profit.
translations.idiomatic: When Vice Minister Li Xun took charge, salt revenues reverted to the Department of Revenue and fictitious valuations ended; nationwide salt sales and tea taxes together yielded six million six hundred fifty thousand strings in net profit.

sentences.zh: 初歲之利，如劉晏之季年，其後則三倍晏時矣。

translations.literal: The profit of the first year equaled Liu Yan's final year; afterward it tripled Yan's time.
translations.idiomatic: First-year profits matched Liu Yan's final year; thereafter they tripled what Yan had achieved.

sentences.zh: 兩池鹽利，歲收百五十餘萬緡。

translations.literal: Two Pools salt profits collected over one million five hundred thousand strings yearly.
translations.idiomatic: The Two Pools alone yielded more than one million five hundred thousand strings a year.

sentences.zh: 四方豪商猾賈，雜處解縣，主以郎官，其佐貳皆御史。

translations.literal: Powerful merchants and crafty traders from all quarters gathered in Jie county; the chief was a court gentleman, his deputies all censors.
translations.idiomatic: Powerful and unscrupulous merchants from every quarter congregated in Jie County; a court gentleman headed the office and censors served as deputies.

sentences.zh: 鹽民田園籍於縣，而令不得以縣民治之。

translations.literal: Salt workers' fields and gardens were registered in the county, yet the magistrate could not treat them as county people in governance.
translations.idiomatic: Salt workers' land remained on county registers, yet magistrates were barred from governing them as ordinary local subjects.

sentences.zh: 憲宗之討淮西也，度支使皇甫鎛加劍南東西兩川、山南西道鹽估以供軍。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xianzong campaigned against Huaixi, Fiscal Commissioner Huangfu Bo raised salt valuations in Eastern and Western Sichuan and Southwest Shannan to supply the army.
translations.idiomatic: During Xianzong's campaign against Huaixi, Fiscal Commissioner Huangfu Bo raised salt assessments in both Sichuan circuits and Southwest Shannan to fund the war.

sentences.zh: 貞元中，盜鬻兩池鹽一石者死，至元和中，減死流天德五城，鎛奏論死如初。

translations.literal: In Zhenyuan times, selling Two Pools salt illegally in the amount of one shi was punished by death; by Yuanhe times this was reduced to exile to Tiande and Wucheng; Bo memorialized to restore death as before.
translations.idiomatic: Under Zhenyuan, smuggling a shi of Two Pools salt meant death; in Yuanhe the penalty was reduced to exile at Tiande and Wucheng until Bo petitioned to restore the death penalty.

sentences.zh: 一斗以上杖背，沒其車驢，能捕斗鹽者賞千錢；

translations.literal: One dou or more—flogging on the back, confiscation of cart and donkey; those who could capture a dou of salt were rewarded one thousand cash;
translations.idiomatic: For a dou or more, offenders were flogged and their carts and donkeys confiscated; informants who seized a dou of illicit salt received one thousand cash in reward.

sentences.zh: 節度觀察使以判官、州以司錄錄事參軍察私鹽，漏一石以上罰課料；

translations.literal: Military governors and observation commissioners used administrative aides; prefectures used registrar-recorder aides to investigate private salt—overlooking one shi or more was punished by forfeiture of salary supplements;
translations.idiomatic: Governors and observation commissioners assigned aides, and prefectures assigned registrars, to hunt private salt; failing to detect a shi or more cost officials their salary supplements.

sentences.zh: 鬻兩池鹽者，坊市居邸主人、市儈皆論坐；

translations.literal: Those who sold Two Pools salt—market ward residents, lodging house owners, and brokers were all prosecuted;
translations.idiomatic: Anyone dealing in Two Pools salt—landlords of ward inns, lodging-house masters, and brokers—was subject to prosecution.

sentences.zh: 盜刮鹻土一斗，比鹽一升。

translations.literal: Stealing and scraping one dou of salty earth was treated as one sheng of salt.
translations.idiomatic: Scraping a dou of salty soil was punished as if one had smuggled a sheng of salt.

sentences.zh: 州縣團保相察，比於貞元加酷矣。

translations.literal: Prefectures and counties had mutual surveillance through collective responsibility groups—harsher than in Zhenyuan.
translations.idiomatic: Prefectures and counties enforced mutual surveillance through neighborhood responsibility groups—harsher even than under Zhenyuan.

sentences.zh: 自兵興，河北鹽法羈縻而已。

translations.literal: Since the rebellion began, the Hebei salt law was merely loosely controlled.
translations.idiomatic: Since the rebellion, Hebei's salt regime had been only loosely enforced.

sentences.zh: 至皇甫鎛又奏置榷鹽使，如江淮榷法，犯禁歲多。

translations.literal: When Huangfu Bo again memorialized to establish salt monopoly commissioners like the Jiang-Huai monopoly law, violations yearly were many.
translations.idiomatic: When Huangfu Bo petitioned to establish salt monopolists in Hebei on the Jiang-Huai model, violations multiplied year by year.

sentences.zh: 及田弘正舉魏博歸朝廷，穆宗命河北罷榷鹽。

translations.literal: When Tian Hongzheng brought Weibo back to the court, Emperor Muzong ordered Hebei to abolish the salt monopoly.
translations.idiomatic: After Tian Hongzheng returned Weibo to imperial control, Muzong abolished the salt monopoly in Hebei.

sentences.zh: 戶部侍郎張平叔議榷鹽法弊，請糶鹽可以富國，詔公卿議其可否。

translations.literal: Vice Minister Zhang Pingshu discussed the defects of the salt monopoly law and petitioned that selling salt could enrich the state; an edict ordered high officials to debate its feasibility.
translations.idiomatic: Vice Minister Zhang Pingshu criticized the monopoly system's abuses and argued that state salt sales could enrich the country; the throne ordered senior officials to debate the proposal.

sentences.zh: 中書舍人韋處厚、兵部侍郎韓愈條詰之，以為不可，平叔屈服。

translations.literal: Secretariat Drafter Wei Chuhou and Vice Minister Han Yu itemized objections, deeming it unfeasible; Pingshu yielded.
translations.idiomatic: Secretariat Drafter Wei Chuhou and Vice Minister Han Yu rebutted the plan point by point and declared it unworkable; Pingshu conceded.

sentences.zh: 是時奉天鹵池生水柏，以灰一斛得鹽十二斤，利倍鹻鹵。

translations.literal: At that time the Fengtian brine pond produced water cypress; one hu of ash yielded twelve jin of salt, profit doubling brine salt.
translations.idiomatic: At that time the Fengtian brine ponds grew water cypress; a hu of burnt ash yielded twelve jin of salt—twice the profit from ordinary brine.

sentences.zh: 文宗時，采灰一斗，比鹽一斤論罪。

translations.literal: In Emperor Wenzong's time, gathering one dou of ash was punished as one jin of salt.
translations.idiomatic: Under Wenzong, collecting a dou of ash was penalized as if one had smuggled a jin of salt.

sentences.zh: 開成末，詔私鹽月再犯者，易縣令，罰刺史俸；

translations.literal: At the end of Kaicheng, an edict: those with private salt violations twice in a month—replace the county magistrate, fine the prefect's salary;
translations.idiomatic: Late in Kaicheng, an edict declared that two private-salt violations within a month would cost a county magistrate his post and dock a prefect's salary.

sentences.zh: 十犯，則罰觀察、判官課料。

translations.literal: Ten violations—then fine the observation commissioner and aide's salary supplements.
translations.idiomatic: Ten violations would forfeit salary supplements from the observation commissioner and his aides.

sentences.zh: 宣宗即位，茶、鹽之法益密，糶鹽少、私盜多者，讁觀察、判官，不計十犯。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xuanzong acceded, tea and salt laws grew stricter; where little official salt was sold and much stolen privately, observation commissioners and aides were demoted, regardless of the ten-violation count.
translations.idiomatic: At Xuanzong's accession tea and salt controls tightened; if official sales lagged while smuggling flourished, observation commissioners and aides were censured without waiting for ten violations.

sentences.zh: 戶部侍郎、判度支盧弘止以兩池鹽法敝，遣巡院官司空輿更立新法，其課倍入，遷榷鹽使。

translations.literal: Vice Minister and Fiscal Affairs adjudicator Lu Hongzhi, finding the Two Pools salt law decayed, dispatched inspection-office official Sikong Yu to establish a new law; revenues doubled, and he was promoted to Salt Monopoly Commissioner.
translations.idiomatic: Fiscal Vice Minister Lu Hongzhi, finding the Two Pools system broken, sent inspection-office official Sikong Yu to draft a new law; revenues doubled and Lu was promoted to Salt Commissioner.

sentences.zh: 以壕籬者，鹽池之隄禁，有盜壞與鬻鹻皆死，鹽盜持弓矢者亦皆死刑。

translations.literal: As for moat-fences—the embankment prohibition of salt ponds—destroying them by theft or selling brine salt were both capital crimes; salt thieves bearing bow and arrow also all received capital punishment.
translations.idiomatic: The moat-fences guarding the salt ponds were sacrosanct: breaking them or selling brine salt meant death, and smugglers caught armed with bow and arrow likewise faced execution.

sentences.zh: 兵部侍郎、判度支周墀又言：「兩池鹽盜販者，迹其居處，保、社按罪。

translations.literal: Vice Minister and Fiscal adjudicator Zhou Chi further said: "For Two Pools salt smugglers, trace their dwelling; collective responsibility groups and communities will fix guilt according to the offense."
translations.idiomatic: Fiscal Vice Minister Zhou Chi added: "When Two Pools salt is smuggled, track the culprits' dwellings and hold ward and community groups liable according to the offense."

sentences.zh: 鬻五石，市二石，亭戶盜糶二石，皆死。

translations.literal: Selling five shi, retailing two shi, pavilion households stealing and selling two shi—all were capital crimes.
translations.idiomatic: Selling five shi, retailing two shi, or pavilion households illicitly selling two shi—all carried the death penalty.

sentences.zh: 」是時江、吳羣盜，以所剽物易茶鹽，不受者焚其室廬，吏不敢枝梧，鎮戍、場鋪、堰埭以關通致富。

translations.literal: At that time bandits in Jiang and Wu exchanged plunder for tea and salt; those who refused had their dwellings burned; officials dared not resist; garrison posts, field stations, dams and ferries grew rich through tolls and passage fees.
translations.idiomatic: At that time Jiang and Wu bandits traded loot for tea and salt; those who refused saw their homes burned, and officials dared not resist. Garrison posts, salt stations, dams, and ferry barriers all grew wealthy charging transit fees.

sentences.zh: 宣宗乃擇嘗更兩畿輔望縣令者為監院官。

translations.literal: Xuanzong then selected men who had served as magistrates of prestigious counties in the two capital regions to be supervisory office officials.
translations.idiomatic: Xuanzong then appointed former magistrates of prominent counties in the capital regions to head the salt inspectorates.

sentences.zh: 戶部侍郎裴休為鹽鐵使，上鹽法八事，其法皆施行，兩池榷課大增。

translations.literal: Vice Minister Pei Xiu became Salt and Iron Commissioner, submitting eight items on the salt law; all were implemented, and Two Pools monopoly revenues greatly increased.
translations.idiomatic: When Vice Minister Pei Xiu became Salt Commissioner he submitted an eight-point salt reform; every measure took effect and Two Pools revenues surged.

sentences.zh: 其後兵遍天下，諸鎮擅利，兩池為河中節度使王重榮所有，歲貢鹽三千車。

translations.literal: Later when warfare spread under heaven, various garrisons monopolized profits; the Two Pools fell to Hezhong Military Governor Wang Chongrong, who yearly presented three thousand cartloads of salt.
translations.idiomatic: Later, as war engulfed the empire and regional armies seized revenues for themselves, the Two Pools passed to Hezhong governor Wang Chongrong, who sent three thousand cartloads of salt in annual tribute.

sentences.zh: 中官田令孜募新軍五十四都，餫轉不足，乃倡議兩池復歸鹽鐵使，而重榮不奉詔，至舉兵反，僖宗為再出，然而卒不能奪。

translations.literal: Eunuch Tian Lingzi recruited fifty-four companies of new troops; transport and supplies were insufficient, so he proposed returning the Two Pools to the Salt and Iron Commission; but Chongrong refused the edict and even raised troops in rebellion; Emperor Xizong marched out twice, yet in the end could not recover them.
translations.idiomatic: Eunuch Tian Lingzi raised fifty-four new army companies but could not supply them, so he proposed restoring the Two Pools to central control; Wang Chongrong defied the edict, took up arms, and even after Emperor Xizong marched against him twice, the court never regained the ponds.

sentences.zh: 唐初無酒禁。

translations.literal: In early Tang there was no prohibition on wine.
translations.idiomatic: Early Tang imposed no restrictions on wine.

sentences.zh: 乾元元年，京師酒貴，肅宗以稟食方屈，乃禁京城酤酒，期以麥熟如初。

translations.literal: First year of Qianyuan, capital wine was expensive; Emperor Suzong, finding grain stores just depleted, prohibited wine-selling in the capital, expecting to restore the old order when wheat ripened.
translations.idiomatic: In 758, as wine prices soared in the capital and grain stores ran low, Suzong banned wine-selling in the capital, promising to lift the ban once the wheat harvest came in.

sentences.zh: 二年，饑，復禁酤，非光祿祭祀、燕蕃客，不御酒。

translations.literal: Second year, famine; wine-selling was again prohibited; except for Grand Provisioner sacrifices and entertaining foreign guests, wine was not consumed at court.
translations.idiomatic: The next year, famine returned and the ban was reimposed; aside from state sacrifices and entertaining foreign envoys, the court itself abstained from wine.

sentences.zh: 廣德二年，定天下酤戶以月收稅。

translations.literal: Second year of Guangde, wine-selling households under heaven were fixed to pay monthly tax.
translations.idiomatic: In 763, wine shops empire-wide were registered to pay a monthly tax.

sentences.zh: 建中元年，罷之。

translations.literal: First year of Jianzhong, this was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: In 780 the tax was abolished.

sentences.zh: 三年，復禁民酤，以佐軍費，置肆釀酒，斛收直三千，州縣總領，醨薄私釀者論其罪。

translations.literal: Third year, private wine-selling was again prohibited to support military expenses; shops were established to brew wine, three thousand cash per hu collected, prefectures and counties overall supervised; thin or privately brewed wine—offenders were prosecuted.
translations.idiomatic: In 782 private wine-selling was banned again to fund the army; government shops brewed wine at three thousand cash per hu under prefectural oversight, and weak or illicit home brewing was prosecuted.

sentences.zh: 尋以京師四方所湊，罷榷。

translations.literal: Soon, because the capital gathered goods from all quarters, the monopoly was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: Soon afterward, since the capital drew goods from every direction, the monopoly was lifted.

sentences.zh: 貞元二年，復禁京城、畿縣酒，天下置肆以酤者，斗錢百五十，免其傜役，獨淮南、忠武、宣武、河東榷麴而已。

translations.literal: Second year of Zhenyuan, wine in the capital and capital counties was again prohibited; under heaven shops selling wine paid one hundred fifty cash per dou, exempt from corvée; only Huainan, Zhongwu, Xuanwu, and Hedong monopolized yeast mash.
translations.idiomatic: In 786 wine was again restricted in the capital and surrounding counties; licensed shops elsewhere paid one hundred fifty cash per dou and were freed from corvée; only Huainan, Zhongwu, Xuanwu, and Hedong retained yeast monopolies.

sentences.zh: 元和六年，罷京師酤肆，以榷酒錢隨兩稅青苗斂之。

translations.literal: Sixth year of Yuanhe, capital wine shops were abolished; wine monopoly money was collected along with the two-tax and green-sprout levies.
translations.idiomatic: In 811 capital wine shops were closed and wine tax was folded into the two-tax and green-sprout assessments.

sentences.zh: 大和八年，遂罷京師榷酤。

translations.literal: Eighth year of Dahe, the capital wine monopoly was finally abolished.
translations.idiomatic: In 834 the capital wine monopoly was abolished entirely.

sentences.zh: 凡天下榷酒為錢百五十六萬餘緡，而釀費居三之一，貧戶逃酤不在焉。

translations.literal: In all, wine monopoly revenue under heaven was one million five hundred sixty thousand strings; brewing costs were one third; poor households evading wine-selling were not counted therein.
translations.idiomatic: Empire-wide wine revenues totaled one million five hundred sixty thousand strings, though brewing costs consumed a third—and poor households who evaded licensed selling were not included in the tally.

sentences.zh: 昭宗世，以用度不足，易京畿近鎮麴法，復榷酒以贍軍，鳳翔節度使李茂貞方顓其利，按兵請入奏利害，天子遽罷之。

translations.literal: In Emperor Zhaozong's time, expenses being insufficient, the yeast law in near capital military districts was exchanged; the wine monopoly was restored to supply the army; Fengxiang Military Governor Li Maozhen just then monopolized its profits, deployed troops and requested audience to discuss pros and cons—the Son of Heaven hurriedly abolished it.
translations.idiomatic: Under Zhaozong, when funds ran short the court swapped yeast regulations in nearby capital districts and revived the wine monopoly to pay the army; Fengxiang governor Li Maozhen, who controlled the profits, marched troops to the capital to argue the policy's merits; the emperor immediately canceled it.

sentences.zh: 初，德宗納戶部侍郎趙贊議，稅天下茶、漆、竹、木，十取一，以為常平本錢。

translations.literal: Initially, Emperor Dezong accepted Vice Minister Zhao Zan's proposal to tax tea, lacquer, bamboo, and wood under heaven at one in ten, as seed money for the Ever-Normal Granary.
translations.idiomatic: Early on, Dezong adopted Vice Minister Zhao Zan's plan to levy a ten-percent tax on tea, lacquer, bamboo, and timber empire-wide to fund the Ever-Normal system.

sentences.zh: 及出奉天，乃悼悔，下詔亟罷之。

translations.literal: When he fled Fengtian, he lamented and repented, issuing an edict urgently abolishing it.
translations.idiomatic: After fleeing to Fengtian he regretted the policy and urgently abolished the levies by edict.

sentences.zh: 及朱泚平，佞臣希意興利者益進。

translations.literal: After Zhu Ci was pacified, sycophantic ministers who sought profit by pleasing the emperor advanced further.
translations.idiomatic: Once Zhu Ci was defeated, flatterers who curried favor by inventing new revenues gained further influence.

sentences.zh: 貞元八年，以水災減稅，明年，諸道鹽鐵使張滂奏：出茶州縣若山及商人要路，以三等定估，十稅其一。

translations.literal: Eighth year of Zhenyuan, taxes were reduced due to flood disaster; the next year, Circuit Salt Commissioner Zhang Pang memorialized: wherever tea was produced in prefectures and counties, in mountains and at merchant thoroughfares, prices were fixed in three grades and taxed one in ten.
translations.idiomatic: In 792 flood relief cut taxes; the next year Commissioner Zhang Pang proposed grading tea by three price tiers at producing counties, mountain districts, and merchant routes, with a ten-percent levy on each.

sentences.zh: 自是歲得錢四十萬緡，然水旱亦未嘗拯之也。

translations.literal: From this yearly revenue reached four hundred thousand strings, yet flood and drought were never relieved by it.
translations.idiomatic: Thereafter the tax yielded four hundred thousand strings annually—yet none of it was ever spent on flood or drought relief.

sentences.zh: 穆宗即位，兩鎮用兵，帑藏空虛，禁中起百尺樓，費不可勝計。

translations.literal: When Emperor Muzong acceded, two garrisons were at war, treasury stores were empty, and within the palace a hundred-foot tower was raised at incalculable expense.
translations.idiomatic: At Muzong's accession two military districts were at war, the treasury stood empty, and the palace began constructing a hundred-foot tower at immeasurable cost.

sentences.zh: 鹽鐵使王播圖寵以自幸，乃增天下茶稅，率百錢增五十。

translations.literal: Salt Commissioner Wang Bo sought favor for himself, and increased tea tax under heaven—on every hundred cash, fifty were added.
translations.idiomatic: Seeking imperial favor, Salt Commissioner Wang Bo raised the tea tax nationwide, adding fifty cash to every hundred owed.

sentences.zh: 江淮、浙東西、嶺南、福建、荊襄茶，播自領之，兩川以戶部領之。

translations.literal: Jiang-Huai, Eastern and Western Zhe, Lingnan, Fujian, and Jing-Xiang tea—Bo personally administered; the Two Sichuan circuits were administered by the Ministry of Revenue.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Bo personally oversaw tea in Jiang-Huai, Zhe East and West, Lingnan, Fujian, and Jing-Xiang; the Ministry of Revenue handled the Two Sichuan circuits.

sentences.zh: 天下茶加斤至二十兩，播又奏加取焉。

translations.literal: Tea under heaven had weight added up to twenty liang per jin; Bo again memorialized for further levies.
translations.idiomatic: Producers were required to add up to twenty liang of weight per jin of tea nationwide, and Bo petitioned for further surcharges.

sentences.zh: 右拾遺李珏上疏諫曰：「榷率起於養兵，今邊境無虞，而厚斂傷民，不可一也。

translations.literal: Right Reminder Li Jue submitted a memorial objecting: "Monopoly rates arose to support the army; now the borders are untroubled, yet heavy levies harm the people—this is unacceptable, first."
translations.idiomatic: Right Reminder Li Jue memorialized in protest: "These monopoly rates were meant to fund the army, yet the frontiers are quiet while heavy levies still burden the people—that alone is reason enough to stop."

sentences.zh: 茗飲，人之所資，重稅則價必增，貧弱益困，不可二也。

translations.literal: "Tea is something people rely on for daily life; heavy tax will necessarily raise prices, the poor and weak will be further distressed—unacceptable, second."
translations.idiomatic: "Tea is a daily necessity; steep taxes will push prices up and squeeze the poor still harder—that is a second reason."

sentences.zh: 山澤之饒，其出不訾，論稅以售多為利，價騰踊則市者稀，不可三也。

translations.literal: "The bounty of mountains and marshes costs nothing to produce; taxing by volume sold maximizes profit, but soaring prices will drive buyers away—unacceptable, third."
translations.idiomatic: "Mountain and marsh produce costs little to harvest; taxing by volume maximizes revenue on paper, but inflated prices will drive buyers away—that is a third reason."

sentences.zh: 」其後王涯判二使，置榷茶使，徙民茶樹於官場，焚其舊積者，天下大怨。

translations.literal: Thereafter Wang Ya judged the two commissions, established a tea monopoly commissioner, relocated commoners' tea trees to government fields, and burned old stockpiles—the people under heaven were greatly resentful.
translations.idiomatic: Later Wang Ya took charge of both commissions, created a tea monopolist, uprooted private tea trees to state fields, and burned old stockpiles—the empire boiled with resentment.

sentences.zh: 令狐楚代為鹽鐵使兼榷茶使，復令納榷，加價而已。

translations.literal: Linghu Chu replaced him as Salt and Iron Commissioner also serving as Tea Monopoly Commissioner, again ordering payment of monopoly dues, merely adding to prices.
translations.idiomatic: Linghu Chu succeeded him as Salt and Tea Commissioner, restoring payment of monopoly dues with nothing more than a price surcharge.

sentences.zh: 李石為相，以茶稅皆歸鹽鐵，復貞元之制。

translations.literal: Li Shi as chief minister, with all tea taxes returning to Salt and Iron, restored the Zhenyuan system.
translations.idiomatic: When Li Shi became chief minister, tea taxes reverted to the Salt Commission and the Zhenyuan system was restored.

sentences.zh: 武宗即位，鹽鐵轉運使崔珙又增江淮茶稅。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wuzong acceded, Salt and Transport Commissioner Cui Gong again increased Jiang-Huai tea tax.
translations.idiomatic: At Wuzong's accession, Transport Commissioner Cui Gong raised Jiang-Huai tea taxes again.

sentences.zh: 是時茶商所過州縣有重稅，或掠奪舟車，露積雨中，諸道置邸以收稅，謂之「搨地錢」，故私販益起。

translations.literal: At that time tea merchants passing through prefectures and counties faced heavy taxes, or had boats and carts plundered, goods piled exposed in rain; various circuits established lodges to collect taxes, called "ground-flattening money"—thus private trafficking increased further.
translations.idiomatic: Tea merchants then faced crushing local levies at every stop; some had boats and carts seized, goods left piled in the rain; circuits set up relay inns to collect what was called "ground-flattening money"—so smuggling only increased.

sentences.zh: 大中初，鹽鐵轉運使裴休著條約：私鬻三犯皆三百斤，乃論死；

translations.literal: At the beginning of the Dazhong era, Pei Xiu, Commissioner for the Transport of Salt and Iron, drafted regulations: for private sale, on three offenses each involving three hundred jin, capital punishment was then imposed;
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Dazhong reign, Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner Pei Xiu issued a code of rules: anyone caught selling tea privately three times, with each offense involving three hundred jin or more, would be sentenced to death;

sentences.zh: 長行羣旅，茶雖少皆死；

translations.literal: For long-distance group travelers, even if the tea was little, all were put to death;
translations.idiomatic: Merchants traveling in large caravans over long routes faced the death penalty even when they carried only a small amount of tea;

sentences.zh: 雇載三犯至五百斤、居舍儈保四犯至千斤者，皆死；

translations.literal: Hired carriers on three offenses reaching five hundred jin, and innkeepers and brokers on four offenses reaching one thousand jin, all were put to death;
translations.idiomatic: Hired haulers convicted three times for amounts up to five hundred jin, and lodging-house keepers and guarantors convicted four times for amounts up to one thousand jin, were all executed;

sentences.zh: 園戶私鬻百斤以上，杖背，三犯，加重傜；

translations.literal: Tea-garden households who privately sold one hundred jin or more were beaten on the back; on three offenses, additional corvée labor was imposed;
translations.idiomatic: Tea growers who sold more than one hundred jin on the black market were flogged; after three convictions, they were subjected to heavier forced labor duties;

sentences.zh: 伐園失業者，刺史、縣令以縱私鹽論。

translations.literal: Where tea gardens were cut down and people lost their livelihood, prefects and county magistrates were prosecuted under the statute for condoning private salt.
translations.idiomatic: If tea gardens were destroyed and growers left without work, the local prefect and county magistrate were held accountable under the same penalties applied for tolerating illicit salt trade.

sentences.zh: 廬、壽、淮南皆加半稅，私商給自首之帖，天下稅茶增倍貞元。

translations.literal: Lu, Shou, and Huainan all had an additional half tax; private merchants were issued certificates of voluntary surrender; empire-wide tea taxes doubled those of the Zhenyuan era.
translations.idiomatic: Lu, Shou, and Huainan each saw their tea levy raised by fifty percent; unauthorized dealers who turned themselves in received official amnesty slips; and nationwide tea revenue came to twice what it had been under the Zhenyuan reign.

sentences.zh: 江淮茶為大摸，一斤至五十兩。

translations.literal: Jianghuai tea was made in large pressed cakes; one jin fetched up to fifty taels.
translations.idiomatic: The finest Jianghuai tea came in large molded cakes, with a single jin selling for as much as fifty taels of silver.

sentences.zh: 諸道鹽鐵使于悰每斤增稅錢五，謂之「剩茶錢」，自是斤兩復舊。

translations.literal: The circuit salt-and-iron commissioners, Yu Cong, added five cash in tax per jin, calling it the "surplus tea levy"; from then on the weight standard returned to the old measure.
translations.idiomatic: Circuit salt-and-iron commissioner Yu Cong imposed an extra five-cash tax on each jin, dubbed the "leftover tea fee," after which the official weight measure was restored to its former standard.

sentences.zh: 凡銀、銅、鐵、錫之冶一百六十八。

translations.literal: In all, there were one hundred sixty-eight smelteries for silver, copper, iron, and tin.
translations.idiomatic: The empire maintained one hundred sixty-eight smelting works for silver, copper, iron, and tin combined.

sentences.zh: 陝、宣、潤、饒、衢、信五州，銀冶五十八，銅冶九十六，鐵山五，錫山二，鉛山四。

translations.literal: In the five prefectures of Shaan, Xuan, Run, Rao, Qu, and Xin: fifty-eight silver smelteries, ninety-six copper smelteries, five iron mines, two tin mines, and four lead mines.
translations.idiomatic: Shaan, Xuan, Run, Rao, Qu, and Xin—the five prefectures together accounted for fifty-eight silver works, ninety-six copper works, five iron mines, two tin mines, and four lead mines.

sentences.zh: 汾州礬山七。

translations.literal: In Fen Prefecture there were seven alum mountains.
translations.idiomatic: Fen Prefecture alone had seven alum-mining sites.

sentences.zh: 麟德二年，廢陝州銅冶四十八。

translations.literal: In the second year of Linde, forty-eight copper smelteries in Shaan Prefecture were abolished.
translations.idiomatic: In 665, forty-eight copper smelting operations in Shaan Prefecture were shut down.

sentences.zh: 開元十五年，初稅伊陽五重山銀、錫。

translations.literal: In the fifteenth year of Kaiyuan, silver and tin from Wuzhong Mountain in Yiyang were first taxed.
translations.idiomatic: In 727, the government began levying taxes on silver and tin mined at Wuzhong Mountain in Yiyang.

sentences.zh: 德宗時戶部侍郎韓洄建議，山澤之利宜歸王者，自是皆隸鹽鐵使。

translations.literal: During the reign of Emperor Dezong, Han Hui, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, proposed that the profits of mountains and marshes ought to belong to the sovereign; from then on all were placed under the Salt and Iron Commissioner.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Dezong, Vice Minister of Revenue Han Hui argued that revenue from mountains and waterways should accrue to the throne; thereafter every such operation fell under the Salt and Iron Commissioner's jurisdiction.

sentences.zh: 元和初，天下銀冶廢者四十，歲采銀萬二千兩，銅二十六萬六千斤，鐵二百七萬斤，錫五萬斤，鉛無常數。

translations.literal: At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, forty silver smelteries throughout the empire had been abolished; annual output was twelve thousand taels of silver, two hundred sixty-six thousand jin of copper, two million seven hundred thousand jin of iron, fifty thousand jin of tin, and lead had no fixed amount.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Yuanhe reign, forty silver works nationwide had already been closed; yearly production stood at twelve thousand taels of silver, two hundred sixty-six thousand jin of copper, two million seven hundred thousand jin of iron, and fifty thousand jin of tin, while lead output was not regularly recorded.

sentences.zh: 開成元年，復以山澤之利歸州縣，刺史選吏主之。

translations.literal: In the first year of Kaicheng, the profits of mountains and marshes were again returned to the prefectures and counties; prefects selected officials to administer them.
translations.idiomatic: In 836, control of mountain and marsh resources was devolved back to local prefectures and counties, with each prefect appointing officials to oversee operations.

sentences.zh: 其後諸州牟利以自殖，舉天下不過七萬餘緡，不能當一縣之茶稅。

translations.literal: Afterward the various prefectures sought profit to enrich themselves; the whole empire yielded no more than seventy thousand-plus strings of cash, which could not equal the tea tax of a single county.
translations.idiomatic: Local prefectures then kept the proceeds for their own benefit, so that empire-wide revenue from these sources never exceeded seventy thousand strings of cash—less than what a single county brought in from tea taxes alone.

sentences.zh: 及宣宗增河湟戍兵衣絹五十二萬餘匹，鹽鐵轉運使裴休請復歸鹽鐵使以供國用，增銀冶二、鐵山七十一，廢銅冶二十七、鉛山一。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xuanzong increased the clothing silk for garrison troops in the Hexi region by five hundred twenty thousand-plus bolts, Pei Xiu, Commissioner for the Transport of Salt and Iron, requested that control be restored to the Salt and Iron Commissioner to supply state needs; two silver smelteries and seventy-one iron mines were added, and twenty-seven copper smelteries and one lead mine were abolished.
translations.idiomatic: After Emperor Xuanzong raised Hexi frontier garrisons' cloth and silk allotments by more than five hundred twenty thousand bolts, Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner Pei Xiu persuaded the court to recentralize mining under the Salt and Iron Commission to fund state expenses—adding two silver works and seventy-one iron mines while closing twenty-seven copper works and one lead mine.

sentences.zh: 天下歲率銀二萬五千兩、銅六十五萬五千斤、鉛十一萬四千斤、錫萬七千斤、鐵五十三萬二千斤。

translations.literal: Empire-wide annual averages were twenty-five thousand taels of silver, six hundred fifty-five thousand jin of copper, one hundred fourteen thousand jin of lead, seventeen thousand jin of tin, and five hundred thirty-two thousand jin of iron.
translations.idiomatic: Under this arrangement the empire annually produced on average twenty-five thousand taels of silver, six hundred fifty-five thousand jin of copper, one hundred fourteen thousand jin of lead, seventeen thousand jin of tin, and five hundred thirty-two thousand jin of iron.

sentences.zh: 隋末行五銖白錢，天下盜起，私鑄錢行。

translations.literal: At the end of the Sui, the white five-zhu coin circulated; bandits rose throughout the empire, and privately cast coins circulated.
translations.idiomatic: In the final years of the Sui dynasty, lightweight five-zhu coins were in use; rebellion spread across the land, and illicit coinage flourished.

sentences.zh: 千錢初重二斤，其後愈輕，不及一斤，鐵葉、皮紙皆以為錢。

translations.literal: One thousand coins initially weighed two jin; afterward they grew ever lighter, falling short of one jin; iron leaves and bark paper were all used as money.
translations.idiomatic: A thousand coins at first weighed two jin, but over time they grew so debased that the same sum weighed less than one jin; people even passed iron scraps and paper as currency.

sentences.zh: 高祖入長安，民間行綫環錢，其製輕小，凡八九萬纔滿半斛。

translations.literal: When Emperor Gaozu entered Chang'an, the people used thread-ring coins; they were made light and small, and only after eighty or ninety thousand did they fill half a hu.
translations.idiomatic: When the founding emperor entered Chang'an, the populace traded in flimsy ring-linked coins so tiny that eighty or ninety thousand of them barely filled half a bushel measure.

sentences.zh: 武德四年，鑄「開元通寶」，徑八分，重二銖四參，積十錢重一兩，得輕重大小之中，其文以八分、篆、隸三體。

translations.literal: In the fourth year of Wude, "Kaiyuan Tongbao" coins were cast: diameter eight fen, weight two zhu four can; ten coins accumulated to one liang in weight, achieving a balance of weight and size; the inscription was rendered in three scripts—regular, seal, and clerical.
translations.idiomatic: In 621 the court minted the Kaiyuan Tongbao coin, eight fen in diameter and two zhu four can in weight, so that ten coins equaled one liang—a carefully calibrated standard—with the legend written in regular, seal, and clerical script forms.

sentences.zh: 洛、幷、幽、益、桂等州皆置監。

translations.literal: Luoyang, Bing, You, Yi, Gui, and other prefectures all established mints.
translations.idiomatic: Mints were established at Luoyang, Bing, You, Yi, Gui, and other major prefectures.

sentences.zh: 賜秦王、齊王三鑪，右僕射裴寂一鑪以鑄。

translations.literal: Three furnaces were granted to the Prince of Qin and the Prince of Qi, and one furnace to Pei Ji, Right Vice Director, for casting.
translations.idiomatic: The Prince of Qin and the Prince of Qi each received three minting furnaces, and Right Vice Director Pei Ji was given one furnace of his own.

sentences.zh: 盜鑄者論死，沒其家屬。

translations.literal: Counterfeiters were sentenced to death, and their households were confiscated.
translations.idiomatic: Anyone caught counterfeiting coins was put to death, and the offender's entire household was seized by the state.

sentences.zh: 其後盜鑄漸起。

translations.literal: Afterward counterfeiting gradually arose.
translations.idiomatic: Before long, illicit coinage began to spread again.

sentences.zh: 顯慶五年，以惡錢多，官為市之，以一善錢售五惡錢，民間藏惡錢以待禁弛。

translations.literal: In the fifth year of Xianqing, because bad coins were numerous, the government purchased them, exchanging one good coin for five bad coins; the people hoarded bad coins awaiting the relaxation of the ban.
translations.idiomatic: In 660, faced with a flood of debased currency, the government offered to buy it up at a rate of one good coin for five bad ones—yet people simply hoarded the inferior coins, betting that enforcement would eventually ease.

sentences.zh: 乾封元年，改鑄「乾封泉寶」錢，徑寸，重二銖六分，以一當舊錢之十。

translations.literal: In the first year of Qianfeng, "Qianfeng Quanbao" coins were recast: diameter one cun, weight two zhu six fen, one counted as ten of the old coins.
translations.idiomatic: In 666 the court replaced the old currency with new Qianfeng Quanbao coins, one cun across and two zhu six fen in weight, each valued at ten of the previous coins.

sentences.zh: 踰年而舊錢多廢，明年，以商賈不通，米帛踊貴，復行開元通寶錢，天下皆鑄之。

translations.literal: After a year the old coins were largely abandoned; the next year, because merchants could not trade and rice and cloth prices soared, Kaiyuan Tongbao coins were restored, and the whole empire cast them.
translations.idiomatic: Within a year most of the old coinage had fallen out of use; the following year commerce ground to a halt and grain and cloth prices spiked, forcing the government to reinstate the Kaiyuan Tongbao and order mints throughout the empire to produce it again.

sentences.zh: 然私錢犯法日蕃，有以舟筏鑄江中者。

translations.literal: Yet violations involving private coinage daily multiplied; some cast coins on boats and rafts in the middle of rivers.
translations.idiomatic: Private minting violations nonetheless multiplied daily, with some counterfeiters operating from boats and rafts moored mid-river.

sentences.zh: 詔所在納惡錢，而姦亦不息。

translations.literal: An edict ordered all localities to accept surrender of bad coins, yet fraud did not cease.
translations.idiomatic: The throne ordered every region to collect and turn in debased coins, but counterfeiting continued unabated.

sentences.zh: 儀鳳中，瀕江民多私鑄錢為業，詔巡江官督捕，載銅、錫、鑞過百斤者沒官。

translations.literal: During the Yifeng era, people along the rivers largely made private coin-casting their occupation; an edict ordered river-patrol officials to supervise arrests, and those transporting copper, tin, or lead in excess of one hundred jin had their goods confiscated by the government.
translations.idiomatic: During the Yifeng reign, riverside communities turned illicit minting into a livelihood; the court dispatched river patrol officers to hunt down offenders and confiscated any shipment of copper, tin, or lead exceeding one hundred jin.

sentences.zh: 四年，命東都糶米粟，斗別納惡錢百，少府、司農毀之。

translations.literal: In the fourth year, the Eastern Capital was ordered to sell grain; for each dou an additional one hundred bad coins were accepted; the Court of the Treasury and the Directorate of Grain destroyed them.
translations.idiomatic: In the fourth year of the era, the Eastern Capital was instructed to sell grain and accept one hundred debased coins per dou as payment, which the Court of the Treasury and the Directorate of Grain then melted down.

sentences.zh: 是時鑄多錢賤，米粟踊貴，乃罷少府鑄，尋復舊。

translations.literal: At this time casting was abundant and coins were cheap, while rice and grain prices soared; the Treasury minting was then abolished, but soon the old practice was restored.
translations.idiomatic: Coin production had become so excessive that money lost value while grain prices climbed; the court briefly shut down Treasury mints, only to reopen them shortly afterward.

sentences.zh: 永淳元年，私鑄者抵死，鄰、保、里、坊、村正皆從坐。

translations.literal: In the first year of Yongchun, private casters were punished by death; neighbors, guarantors, ward heads, lane heads, and village chiefs were all implicated.
translations.idiomatic: In 682 anyone who minted coins privately faced the death penalty, and neighbors, guarantors, block wardens, lane overseers, and village heads were all held liable as accomplices.

sentences.zh: 武后時，錢非穿穴及鐵錫銅液，皆得用之，熟銅、排斗、沙澀之錢皆售，自是盜鑄蜂起，江淮游民依大山陂海以鑄，吏莫能捕。

translations.literal: During the reign of Empress Wu, coins without holes and those of iron, tin, and copper slag were all permitted for use; worked copper coins, stacked coins, and gritty coins were all sold; from then counterfeiting swarmed forth, and vagrants of the Jianghuai region relied on great mountains, marshes, and the sea to cast coins; officials could not capture them.
translations.idiomatic: Under Empress Wu, even unholed coins and pieces cast from iron, tin, and copper slag circulated freely, and worn copper of every inferior grade found buyers; counterfeiting then exploded, as Jianghuai drifters set up hidden mints in remote mountains, marshes, and along the coast, beyond the reach of local officials.

sentences.zh: 先天之際，兩京錢益濫，郴、衡錢纔有輪郭，鐵錫五銖之屬皆可用之。

translations.literal: At the time of Xiantian, coins in the two capitals grew ever more debased; coins of Chen and Heng barely had rims; iron, tin, and five-zhu types were all usable.
translations.idiomatic: By the Xiantian era, currency in the two capitals had become severely debased; coins from Chen and Heng were so crude they barely had rims, and iron, tin, and five-zhu pieces all passed as legal tender.

sentences.zh: 或鎔錫摸錢，須臾百十。

translations.literal: Some melted tin and molded coins; in an instant one hundred or ten were produced.
translations.idiomatic: Some counterfeiters simply melted tin and cast coins from molds, turning out a hundred or more in moments.

sentences.zh: 開元初，宰相宋璟請禁惡錢，行二銖四參錢，毀舊錢不可用者。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Kaiyuan, Chancellor Song Jing requested a ban on bad coins, circulation of two-zhu four-can coins, and destruction of old coins that could not be used.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Kaiyuan reign, Chancellor Song Jing proposed outlawing debased currency, enforcing the two-zhu four-can standard, and recalling and melting down all unusable old coins.

sentences.zh: 江淮有官鑪錢、偏鑪錢、稜錢、時錢，遣監察御史蕭隱之使江淮，率戶出惡錢，捕責甚峻，上青錢皆輸官，小惡者沈江湖，市井不通，物價益貴，隱之坐貶官。

translations.literal: In the Jianghuai region there were official-furnace coins, off-furnace coins, rimmed coins, and current coins; the censor Xiao Yinzhí was dispatched to the Jianghuai region to lead households in surrendering bad coins; arrests and penalties were extremely severe; superior greenish coins were all delivered to the government, and lesser bad ones were sunk in rivers and lakes; markets could not function, and prices grew ever costlier; Yinzhí was demoted for his offense.
translations.idiomatic: The Jianghuai region was awash in official-mint coins, off-spec furnace pieces, rimmed coins, and assorted contemporary issues; the court sent Censor Xiao Yinzhí to compel every household to surrender debased currency under harsh enforcement—fine greenish coins went to the treasury while inferior ones were dumped in rivers and lakes; commerce seized up, prices soared, and Yinzhí himself was demoted for the fiasco.

sentences.zh: 宋璟又請出米十萬斛收惡錢，少府毀之。

translations.literal: Song Jing again requested the release of one hundred thousand hu of grain to purchase bad coins, which the Court of the Treasury would destroy.
translations.idiomatic: Song Jing then proposed releasing one hundred thousand hu of grain to buy up debased coins for the Treasury to melt down.

sentences.zh: 十一年，詔所在加鑄，禁賣銅錫及造銅器者。

translations.literal: In the eleventh year, an edict ordered all localities to increase casting and banned the sale of copper and tin and the manufacture of copper vessels.
translations.idiomatic: In the eleventh year of Kaiyuan, the throne ordered every region to step up coin production while prohibiting the sale of copper and tin and the making of copper goods.

sentences.zh: 二十年，千錢以重六斤四兩為率，每錢重二銖四參，禁缺頓、沙澀、盪染、白彊、黑彊之錢。

translations.literal: In the twentieth year, one thousand coins were set at a standard weight of six jin four liang; each coin weighed two zhu four can; coins that were chipped, gritty, washed, white-streaked, or black-streaked were banned.
translations.idiomatic: In 732 the standard was fixed at six jin four liang per thousand coins, or two zhu four can each, and chipped, gritty, tampered, white-streaked, and black-streaked coins were outlawed.

sentences.zh: 首者，官為市之。

translations.literal: Informants—the government purchased the coins from them.
translations.idiomatic: Those who reported violations had their seized coins bought up by the government.

sentences.zh: 銅一斤為錢八十。

translations.literal: One jin of copper made eighty coins.
translations.idiomatic: Each jin of copper was allotted to produce eighty coins.

sentences.zh: 二十二年，宰相張九齡建議：「古者以布帛菽粟不可尺寸抄勺而均，乃為錢以通貿易。

translations.literal: In the twenty-second year, Chancellor Zhang Jiuling proposed: "In antiquity, because cloth, silk, beans, and grain could not be measured and divided evenly by the inch or the dipper, coins were made to facilitate trade.
translations.idiomatic: In 734 Chancellor Zhang Jiuling argued: "In ancient times cloth, silk, grain, and beans could not be apportioned precisely by measure, so coinage was invented to grease the wheels of commerce.

sentences.zh: 官鑄所入無幾，而工費多，宜縱民鑄。

translations.literal: Revenue from official casting was slight, while labor costs were great; private casting by the people ought to be permitted.
translations.idiomatic: State mints bring in little while costing a fortune to run—the better course is to let the people mint coins themselves.

sentences.zh: 」議下百官，宰相裴耀卿、黃門侍郎李林甫、河南少尹蕭炅、祕書監崔沔皆以為「嚴斷惡錢則人知禁，稅銅折役則官冶可成，計估度庸則私錢以利薄而自息。

translations.literal: " The proposal was sent down to the hundred officials; Chancellor Pei Yaoji, Vice Director of the Yellow Gate Li Linfu, Vice Prefect of Henan Xiao Jiong, and Director of the Secretariat Cui Hong all held that "if bad coins are strictly cut off, people will know the prohibition; if copper is taxed and corvée converted, official smelting can succeed; if valuation and corvée substitution are calculated, private coinage will cease of itself because profits are thin.
translations.idiomatic: " The proposal went before the full bureaucracy. Chancellor Pei Yaoji, Vice Director of the Yellow Gate Li Linfu, Vice Prefect of Henan Xiao Jiong, and Secretariat Director Cui Hong all countered that strict suppression of debased coinage would teach people to obey the law; taxing copper and converting labor dues would make state smelting viable; and setting valuation standards for corvée would starve private minting of its profit margin.

sentences.zh: 若許私鑄，則下皆棄農而競利矣」。

translations.literal: If private casting is permitted, then those below will all abandon farming and compete for profit."
translations.idiomatic: Allow private minting, and the common people will abandon the plow for the lure of easy coin."

sentences.zh: 左監門衞錄事參軍事劉秩曰：「今之錢，古之下幣也。

translations.literal: Left Supervisor of the Gate Guard Regiment Records Officer Liu Zhi said: "Today's coins are the inferior currency of antiquity."
translations.idiomatic: Liu Zhi, a records officer in the Left Gate Guard Regiment, said: "Money today is what the ancients called the lowest grade of currency."

sentences.zh: 若捨之任人，則上無以御下，下無以事上，不可一也。

translations.literal: If one abandons it and lets people do as they please, then above will have no means to govern those below, and those below will have no means to serve those above—this may not be done, reason one.
translations.idiomatic: If the state renounces control and leaves minting to private hands, the throne loses leverage over its subjects and subjects lose their basis for serving the throne. That alone is sufficient reason to forbid it.

sentences.zh: 物賤傷農，錢輕傷賈，物重則錢輕，錢輕由乎物多，多則作法收之使少，物少則作法布之使輕，奈何假人？

translations.literal: When goods are cheap it injures farmers; when money is light it injures merchants. When goods are heavy in price, money is light; money becomes light because goods are many—when many, one uses methods to collect them and make them few; when goods are few, one uses methods to distribute them and make money light—why entrust this to others?
translations.idiomatic: Cheap produce ruins farmers; debased coinage ruins traders. When goods are plentiful, money loses value—and the remedy is to absorb surplus goods, not flood the market with coin. When goods are scarce, the state should release money to ease prices. Why would we hand that power to private minters?

sentences.zh: 不可二也。

translations.literal: This may not be done—reason two.
translations.idiomatic: That is the second reason it must be rejected.

sentences.zh: 鑄錢不雜鉛鐵則無利，雜則錢惡。

translations.literal: Minting coins without mixing in lead and iron yields no profit; mix them in and the coins are debased.
translations.idiomatic: Coin minting turns a profit only by adulterating the metal, and adulteration produces bad money.

sentences.zh: 今塞私鑄之路，人猶冒死，況設陷穽誘之？

translations.literal: Today, with the path to private minting blocked, people still risk death—how much more if one sets snares to lure them?
translations.idiomatic: Even with private minting outlawed, people still risk execution to do it—how much worse would it be if the law openly baited them with profit?

sentences.zh: 不可三也。

translations.literal: This may not be done—reason three.
translations.idiomatic: That is the third objection.

sentences.zh: 鑄錢無利則人不鑄，有利則去南畝者眾，不可四也。

translations.literal: When coin minting yields no profit, people will not mint; when there is profit, many will leave the southern fields—this may not be done, reason four.
translations.idiomatic: If minting pays nothing, no one will do it; if it pays well, peasants will abandon the fields in droves. That is the fourth reason to forbid it.

sentences.zh: 人富則不可以賞勸，貧則不可以威禁。

translations.literal: When people are wealthy, rewards cannot encourage them; when poor, punishments cannot restrain them.
translations.idiomatic: The rich cannot be moved by reward, and the poor cannot be governed by fear of punishment.

sentences.zh: 法不行，人不理，繇貧富不齊。

translations.literal: Laws are not enforced, people are not orderly, because wealth and poverty are uneven.
translations.idiomatic: When wealth and poverty diverge too sharply, law loses force and society falls out of order.

sentences.zh: 若得鑄錢，貧者服役於富室，富室乘而益恣，不可五也。

translations.literal: If private minting were allowed, the poor would serve in wealthy houses, and the wealthy would take advantage and grow more arbitrary—this may not be done, reason five.
translations.idiomatic: If minting were permitted, the poor would become bondsmen to the rich, and the wealthy would exploit the power of coin to act with even greater impunity. That is the fifth reason.

sentences.zh: 夫錢重繇人日滋於前，而鑪不加舊。

translations.literal: As for heavy coin, it daily multiplied before the people, while the number of furnaces was not increased from former levels.
translations.idiomatic: Full-weight coin kept piling up in private hands, yet the number of official mints had not grown since earlier times.

sentences.zh: 公錢與銅價頗等，故破重錢為輕錢，銅之不贍，在採用者眾也。

translations.literal: Official coins and the price of copper were roughly equal; therefore heavy coins were broken into light ones; copper's insufficiency lay in the many who used it.
translations.idiomatic: Because official coin was worth nearly its weight in raw copper, people melted good coins into bad ones—and copper ran short simply because too many hands competed for it.

sentences.zh: 銅之為兵不如鐵，為器不如漆。

translations.literal: Copper for weapons is not as good as iron; for vessels not as good as lacquer.
translations.idiomatic: Copper makes inferior weapons compared with iron, and inferior utensils compared with lacquerware.

sentences.zh: 禁銅則人無所用，盜鑄者少，公錢不破，人不犯死，錢又日增，是一舉而四美兼也。

translations.literal: Ban copper and people have no use for it; illicit minters will be few; official coins will not be broken down; people will not risk death; coins will daily increase—one act and four blessings combined.
translations.idiomatic: Ban private use of copper, and copper stops draining into illicit mints; official coin stops being melted down, counterfeiting drops, and the supply of sound money grows—all from a single policy yielding four gains at once.

sentences.zh: 」是時公卿皆以縱民鑄為不便，於是下詔禁惡錢而已。

translations.literal: At that time all high officials held that allowing the people to mint was inconvenient; thereupon an edict was issued banning debased coins, and that was all.
translations.idiomatic: At that point the court overwhelmingly agreed that private minting was a bad idea, and the emperor issued an edict banning debased coin—nothing more.

sentences.zh: 信安郡王禕復言國用不足，請縱私鑄，議者皆畏禕帝弟之貴，莫敢與抗，獨倉部郎中韋伯陽以為不可，禕議亦格。

translations.literal: Prince of Xin'an Commandery Li Yi again said state funds were insufficient and requested allowing private minting; those debating all feared Li Yi's honor as the emperor's younger brother and none dared oppose him; only Bureau of Granaries Director Wei Boyang held it could not be done, and Li Yi's proposal was also blocked.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Xin'an, Li Yi, raised the shortage of revenue again and asked to legalize private minting. Debates fell silent—few dared contest an imperial prince—until Wei Boyang of the Granaries Bureau alone objected, and Li Yi's plan was set aside.

sentences.zh: 二十六年，宣、潤等州初置錢監，兩京用錢稍善，米粟價益下。

translations.literal: In the twenty-sixth year, Xuan, Run, and other prefectures first established coin supervisors; coin in the two capitals became somewhat better, and grain prices steadily fell.
translations.idiomatic: In Kaiyuan 26, new mint supervisors were established in Xuancheng, Runzhou, and elsewhere; currency in both capitals improved, and grain prices dropped.

sentences.zh: 其後錢又漸惡，詔出銅所在置監，鑄開元通寶錢，京師庫藏皆滿。

translations.literal: Afterward coins again gradually deteriorated; an edict ordered supervisors established wherever copper was exported, casting Kaiyuan Tongbao coins; the capital storehouses were all filled.
translations.idiomatic: Debasement returned; the throne ordered mints wherever copper was mined to cast Kaiyuan Tongbao, until the capital treasuries overflowed.

sentences.zh: 天下盜鑄益起，廣陵、丹楊、宣城尤甚。

translations.literal: Throughout the realm illicit minting increasingly arose; Guangling, Danyang, and Xuancheng were especially severe.
translations.idiomatic: Counterfeiting spread empire-wide, worst in Yangzhou, Danyang, and Xuancheng.

sentences.zh: 京師權豪，歲歲取之，舟車相屬。

translations.literal: Powerful families of the capital took them year after year, boats and carts following one after another.
translations.idiomatic: Capital elites bought up debased coin year after year, with convoys of boats and carts rolling in without pause.

sentences.zh: 江淮偏鑪錢數十種，雜以鐵錫，輕漫無復錢形。

translations.literal: Along the Yangzi and Huai there were dozens of types of private-furnace coins, mixed with iron and tin, light and flimsy until they no longer resembled coins in shape.
translations.idiomatic: Private mints along the Yangzi-Huai corridor produced dozens of varieties adulterated with iron and tin—so thin and crude they barely looked like money.

sentences.zh: 公鑄者號官鑪錢，一以當偏鑪錢七八，富商往往藏之，以易江淮私鑄者。

translations.literal: Those publicly cast were called official-furnace coins; one could exchange for seven or eight private-furnace coins; wealthy merchants often hoarded them to trade for Yangzi-Huai private casts.
translations.idiomatic: Official coin bought seven or eight private coins; merchants hoarded the good stuff and traded it for cheap Yangzi counterfeits.

sentences.zh: 兩京錢有鵝眼、古文、綫環之別，每貫重不過三四斤，至翦鐵而緡之。

translations.literal: Coin in the two capitals had the varieties goose-eye, ancient script, and thread-ring; each string weighed no more than three or four jin, reaching the point of cutting iron and stringing it.
translations.idiomatic: Capitals circulated goose-eye, ancient-script, and thread-ring coin—each thousand-coin string weighing barely three or four pounds—until people were stringing clipped iron as cash.

sentences.zh: 宰相李林甫請出絹布三百萬匹，平估收錢，物價踊貴，訴者日萬人。

translations.literal: Chancellor Li Linfu requested releasing three million bolts of silk and cloth, collecting coins at fair valuation; goods prices leaped high; complainants numbered ten thousand per day.
translations.idiomatic: Chancellor Li Linfu proposed releasing three million bolts of silk and cloth to buy up coin at assessed rates, but prices spiked and ten thousand petitioners poured in daily.

sentences.zh: 兵部侍郎楊國忠欲招權以市恩，揚鞭市門曰：「行當復之。

translations.literal: Vice Minister of War Yang Guozhong wished to win power by currying favor; he raised a whip at the market gate and said: "It will soon be restored."
translations.idiomatic: Yang Guozhong, Vice Minister of War, sought to seize favor by playing savior; whip in hand at the market gate he promised: "The old currency will be restored."

sentences.zh: 」明日，詔復行舊錢。

translations.literal: The next day, an edict restored circulation of the old coins.
translations.idiomatic: The next day an edict restored the previous coin standard.

sentences.zh: 天寶十一載，又出錢三十萬緡易兩市惡錢，出左藏庫排斗錢，許民易之。

translations.literal: In the eleventh year of Tianbao, three hundred thousand strings of coins were again released to exchange for debased coin in the two markets; piled-and-sorted coins from the Left Treasury were released, allowing the people to exchange for them.
translations.idiomatic: In Tianbao 11, the court spent three hundred thousand strings to swap out bad money in the markets, issuing sorted coin from the Left Treasury for public exchange.

sentences.zh: 國忠又言錢非鐵錫、銅沙、穿穴、古文，皆得用之。

translations.literal: Guozhong further said that coins need not exclude iron-tin, copper sand, pierced holes, and ancient script—all could be used.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Guozhong went further, declaring that coin adulterated with iron, tin, copper slag, holes, or worn ancient inscriptions should all remain legal tender.

sentences.zh: 是時增調農人鑄錢，既非所習，皆不聊生。

translations.literal: At this time farmers were additionally levied to mint coins; it was not what they were skilled at, and all were unable to make a living.
translations.idiomatic: Farmers conscripted into mint labor knew nothing of the craft and could barely survive.

sentences.zh: 內作判官韋倫請厚價募工，繇是役用減而鼓鑄多。

translations.literal: Palace Workshop Judge Wei Lun requested recruiting workers at high wages; thereby corvée labor was reduced while coin casting increased.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Lun of the Palace Workshops proposed hiring skilled workers at premium wages, cutting forced peasant labor while boosting output.

sentences.zh: 天下鑪九十九：絳州三十，揚、潤、宣、鄂、蔚皆十，益、郴皆五，洋州三，定州一。

translations.literal: Throughout the realm there were ninety-nine furnaces: thirty in Jiang Prefecture; Yang, Run, Xuan, E, and Yu each ten; Yi and Chen each five; Yang Prefecture three; Ding Prefecture one.
translations.idiomatic: Ninety-nine mints operated empire-wide: thirty at Jiangzhou; ten each at Yangzhou, Runzhou, Xuancheng, Ezhou, and Yuzhou; five each at Yizhou and Chenzhou; three at Yang Prefecture; one at Dingzhou.

sentences.zh: 每鑪歲鑄錢三千三百緡，役丁匠三十，費銅二萬一千二百斤、鑞三千七百斤、錫五百斤。

translations.literal: Each furnace yearly cast three thousand three hundred strings of coin, employing thirty laborers and artisans, consuming twenty-one thousand two hundred jin of copper, three thousand seven hundred jin of lead, and five hundred jin of tin.
translations.idiomatic: Each mint produced 3,300 strings a year with thirty workers, consuming 21,200 jin of copper, 3,700 jin of lead, and 500 jin of tin.

sentences.zh: 每千錢費錢七百五十。

translations.literal: Every thousand coins cost seven hundred fifty coins to produce.
translations.idiomatic: Minting cost seven hundred fifty cash per thousand produced.

sentences.zh: 天下歲鑄三十二萬七千緡。

translations.literal: Throughout the realm yearly casting was three hundred twenty-seven thousand strings.
translations.idiomatic: Empire-wide annual output reached 327,000 strings.

sentences.zh: 肅宗乾元元年，經費不給，鑄錢使第五琦鑄「乾元重寶」錢，徑一寸，每緡重十斤，與開元通寶參用，以一當十，亦號「乾元十當錢」。

translations.literal: In Emperor Suzong's first year of Qianyuan, expenses were insufficient; Coinage Commissioner Diwu Qi cast "Qianyuan Heavy Treasure" coins, one inch in diameter, each string weighing ten jin; used together with Kaiyuan Tongbao, one counted as ten—also called "Qianyuan Ten-Count Coins."
translations.idiomatic: In Qianyuan 1, with the treasury empty, Coinage Commissioner Diwu Qi introduced the Qianyuan Heavy Treasure—one inch across, ten pounds per string—valued at ten Kaiyuan coins and nicknamed the "ten-for-one Qianyuan."

sentences.zh: 先是諸鑪鑄錢窳薄，鎔破錢及佛像，謂之「盤陀」，皆鑄為私錢，犯者杖死。

translations.literal: Earlier the various furnaces cast coins thin and poor; melting broken coins and Buddha images, called "pántuó," all were cast as private coin; violators were beaten to death.
translations.idiomatic: Official mints had already been producing thin coin; people melted scrap coin and bronze Buddhas—"pántuó"—into counterfeits, a capital offense.

sentences.zh: 第五琦為相，復命絳州諸鑪鑄重輪乾元錢，徑一寸二分，其文亦曰「乾元重寶」，背之外郭為重輪，每緡重十二斤，與開元通寶錢並行，以一當五十。

translations.literal: When Diwu Qi became chancellor, he again ordered the Jiang Prefecture furnaces to cast heavy-rim Qianyuan coins, one inch two fen in diameter; the inscription also read "Qianyuan Heavy Treasure"; on the back the outer rim was a double rim; each string weighed twelve jin; circulated together with Kaiyuan Tongbao, one counted as fifty.
translations.idiomatic: As chancellor, Diwu Qi ordered Jiangzhou mints to produce double-rim Qianyuan Heavy Treasure coin—slightly larger, twelve pounds per string—worth fifty Kaiyuan coins apiece.

sentences.zh: 是時民間行三錢，大而重稜者亦號「重稜錢」。

translations.literal: At this time three kinds of coin circulated among the people; the large ones with heavy rims were also called "heavy-rim coins."
translations.idiomatic: Three coin types circulated side by side; the large double-rim pieces were known as "heavy-rim money."

sentences.zh: 法既屢易，物價騰踊，米斗錢至七千，餓死者滿道。

translations.literal: Since the laws had repeatedly changed, goods prices surged; a dou of rice reached seven thousand coins; starved dead filled the roads.
translations.idiomatic: Constant currency reversals sent prices soaring—a peck of rice hit seven thousand cash, and corpses of the starved lined the streets.

sentences.zh: 初有「虛錢」，京師人人私鑄，併小錢，壞鍾、像，犯禁者愈眾。

translations.literal: At first there was "nominal coin"; in the capital everyone privately minted, combining small coins, destroying bells and images; violators of the prohibition grew ever more numerous.
translations.idiomatic: "Nominal money" appeared first; everyone in the capital counterfeited small coin by melting bells and statues, and prosecutions multiplied.

sentences.zh: 鄭叔清為京兆尹，數月榜死者八百餘人。

translations.literal: Zheng Shuqing served as Governor of Jingzhao; within several months those flogged to death numbered more than eight hundred.
translations.idiomatic: As Jingzhao governor, Zheng Shuqing had more than eight hundred offenders beaten to death in just a few months.

sentences.zh: 肅宗以新錢不便，命百官集議，不能改。

translations.literal: Emperor Suzong, finding the new coins inconvenient, ordered the hundred officials to assemble and deliberate; they could not change it.
translations.idiomatic: Suzong, acknowledging the new currency's failure, convened the court for reform—and achieved nothing.

sentences.zh: 上元元年，減重輪錢以一當三十，開元舊錢與乾元十當錢，皆以一當十，碾磑鬻受，得為實錢，虛錢交易皆用十當錢，由是錢有虛實之名。

translations.literal: In the first year of Shangyuan, heavy-rim coins were reduced to one counting as thirty; old Kaiyuan and Qianyuan ten-count coins both counted as ten; ground and milled, sold and accepted, could serve as real coin; nominal-coin transactions all used ten-count coin—whereby coin acquired the names "nominal" and "real."
translations.idiomatic: In Shangyuan 1, double-rim coin was cut to thirty-for-one, while old Kaiyuan and ten-count Qianyuan were pegged at ten-for-one; worn coin ground down could still pass as "real money," but nominal transactions ran on ten-count pieces—thus "real" and "nominal" coin entered the language.

sentences.zh: 史思明據東都，亦鑄「得一元寶」錢，徑一寸四分，以一當開元通寶之百。
