translations.literal: Shi Siming held the Eastern Capital and also cast "De Yi Yuanbao" coins, one inch four fen in diameter, one counting as one hundred Kaiyuan Tongbao.
translations.idiomatic: Rebels under Shi Siming, holding Luoyang, minted the "De Yi Yuanbao"—large coins worth a hundred Kaiyuan each.

sentences.zh: 既而惡「得一」非長祚之兆，改其文曰「順天元寶」。

translations.literal: Soon afterward they disliked that "de yi" (obtain one) was not an omen of long reign; the inscription was changed to read "Shuntian Yuanbao."
translations.idiomatic: Siming soon scrapped the name—the character for "obtain" seemed an ill omen for a lasting dynasty—and renamed the coin "Shuntian Yuanbao" (Obedient to Heaven).

sentences.zh: 代宗即位，乾元重寶錢以一當二，重輪錢以一當三，凡三日而大小錢皆以一當一。

translations.literal: When Emperor Daizong ascended, Qianyuan Heavy Treasure counted as two; heavy-rim coins counted as three; within three days large and small coins all counted as one for one.
translations.idiomatic: Upon Daizong's accession, Qianyuan was devalued to two-for-one and double-rim to three-for-one; within three days every denomination returned to face value.

sentences.zh: 自第五琦更鑄，犯法者日數百，州縣不能禁止，至是人甚便之。

translations.literal: Since Diwu Qi's recoinage, lawbreakers numbered hundreds daily; prefectures and counties could not forbid it; by this time people found it greatly convenient.
translations.idiomatic: From Diwu Qi's reforms onward, hundreds broke the coin laws daily and local officials could not stop them—yet when denominations unified, the public welcomed the relief.

sentences.zh: 其後民間乾元、重稜二錢鑄為器，不復出矣。

translations.literal: Afterward among the people Qianyuan and heavy-rim coins were both cast into utensils and no longer circulated.
translations.idiomatic: Qianyuan and heavy-rim coin soon disappeared from circulation, melted down for household ware.

sentences.zh: 當時議者以為「自天寶至今，戶九百餘萬。

translations.literal: Contemporary debaters held that "From Tianbao until now, households exceed nine million."
translations.idiomatic: Policy critics observed: "From the Tianbao era to the present, registered households exceed nine million."

sentences.zh: 王制：上農夫食九人，中農夫七人。

translations.literal: The Royal Regulations: a superior farmer feeds nine persons; a middle farmer feeds seven.
translations.idiomatic: As the Royal Regulations put it, a first-rate cultivator can support nine people and a middling one seven.

sentences.zh: 以中農夫計之，為六千三百萬人。

translations.literal: Calculated by the middle farmer standard, this comes to sixty-three million persons.
translations.idiomatic: Figuring by the middling cultivator's yield, that works out to sixty-three million people.

sentences.zh: 少壯相均，人食米二升，日費米百二十六萬斛，歲費四萬五千三百六十萬斛，而衣倍之，吉凶之禮再倍，餘三年之儲以備水旱凶災，當米十三萬六千八十萬斛，以貴賤豐儉相當，則米之直與錢鈞也。

translations.literal: With young and strong evenly balanced, each person eats two sheng of rice; daily rice expenditure is 1,260,000 hu, yearly 453,600,000 hu; clothing doubles this, auspicious and inauspicious rites double it again, and a three-year reserve against flood, drought, and disaster requires 1,360,800,000 hu of rice; when high and low, plenty and scarcity are balanced, then the price of rice and coin will be equal.
translations.idiomatic: Assuming a balanced mix of adults in their prime, at two sheng of rice per person per day, daily consumption would run to 1.26 million hu and yearly to 453.6 million hu. Double that for clothing, double it again for weddings and funerals, and set aside enough grain for three years against flood, drought, and famine—1.368 billion hu in all. When rank and wealth, abundance and want are properly aligned, the value of grain and cash should stand in equilibrium.

sentences.zh: 田以高下肥瘠豐耗為率，一頃出米五十餘斛，當田二千七百二十一萬六千頃。

translations.literal: Fields are rated by elevation, fertility, and harvest yield; one qing yields fifty-odd hu of rice, requiring 27,216,000 qing of farmland.
translations.idiomatic: Taking fields by their grade of elevation, soil, and output, and assuming roughly fifty hu of rice per qing, the empire would need some 27.2 million qing under the plow.

sentences.zh: 而錢亦歲毀於棺瓶埋藏焚溺，其間銅貴錢賤，有鑄以為器者，不出十年錢幾盡，不足周當世之用」。

translations.literal: Yet coin is also yearly destroyed in coffins, jars, burial, burning, and drowning; meanwhile copper is costly and coin cheap, and some cast it into vessels—in less than ten years coin will nearly be exhausted, insufficient to meet the needs of the age."
translations.idiomatic: Coin is also lost every year to coffins, urns, burial hoards, fire, and water. With copper dear and cash cheap, people melt coin to cast utensils; within a decade the currency will be all but gone, unable to sustain the economy of the day."

sentences.zh: 諸道鹽鐵轉運使劉晏以江、嶺諸州，任土所出，皆重粗賤弱之貨，輸京師不足以供道路之直。

translations.literal: Circuit salt-and-iron transport commissioner Liu Yan held that in the Jiang and Ling prefectures, whatever each region produced was heavy, crude, cheap, inferior goods whose shipment to the capital could not even cover transport costs.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Yan, commissioner for salt-and-iron transport across the circuits, observed that the Jiang and Ling regions shipped only bulky, low-grade local goods to the capital—goods so worthless that freight alone consumed their value.

sentences.zh: 於是積之江淮，易銅鉛薪炭，廣鑄錢，歲得十餘萬緡，輸京師及荊、揚二州，自是錢日增矣。

translations.literal: Thereupon he stockpiled goods at the Jiang-Huai, exchanged them for copper, lead, fuel, and charcoal, expanded coin casting, and gained over 100,000 strings per year, sending them to the capital and to Jing and Yang prefectures; from then on coin daily increased.
translations.idiomatic: He therefore accumulated those goods along the Yangzi and Huai, traded them for copper, lead, and fuel, and stepped up minting, producing more than a hundred thousand strings a year for the capital and for Jing and Yang. From that point the money supply steadily grew.

sentences.zh: 大曆七年，禁天下鑄銅器。

translations.literal: In the seventh year of Dali, the empire was forbidden to cast copper vessels.
translations.idiomatic: In Dali 7, a ban on casting copper utensils was imposed throughout the realm.

sentences.zh: 建中初，戶部侍郎韓洄以商州紅崖冶銅多，請復洛源廢監，起十鑪，歲鑄錢七萬二千緡，每千錢費九百。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Jianzhong, Vice Minister of Revenue Han Hui, noting that Shangzhou's Hongya smeltery had abundant copper, requested restoration of the abandoned Luoyuan mint, the opening of ten furnaces, yearly casting of 72,000 strings, at a cost of nine hundred per thousand coins.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Jianzhong era, Han Hui of the Ministry of Revenue, citing the rich copper deposits at Shangzhou's Hongya works, petitioned to reopen the defunct Luoyuan mint with ten furnaces, aiming to coin seventy-two thousand strings a year at a minting cost of nine hundred cash per thousand.

sentences.zh: 德宗從之。

translations.literal: Emperor Dezong assented.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Dezong approved the plan.

sentences.zh: 江淮多鉛錫錢，以銅盪外，不盈斤兩，帛價益貴。

translations.literal: In the Jiang-Huai there was much lead-and-tin coin; the copper was rinsed off the outside, not filling a full jin or liang, and silk prices grew ever costlier.
translations.idiomatic: Lead-tin coins flooded the Jiang-Huai region—thin copper wash on the surface, barely a full ounce of metal in each—and the price of silk kept climbing.

sentences.zh: 銷千錢為銅六斤，鑄器則斤得錢六百，故銷鑄者多，而錢益耗。

translations.literal: Melting a thousand coins yields six jin of copper; cast into vessels, one jin returns six hundred coins in value—hence many melted and recast, and coin grew ever scarcer.
translations.idiomatic: A thousand coins melted down gave six pounds of copper, but that same copper cast into ware could pass for six hundred coins' worth—so melting flourished and the currency bled away.

sentences.zh: 判度支趙贊採連州白銅鑄大錢，一當十，以權輕重。

translations.literal: Budget commissioner Zhao Zan took white copper from Lianzhou to cast large coins, each counted as ten, to adjust light and heavy.
translations.idiomatic: Zhao Zan, who oversaw the budget, drew on Lianzhou's white copper to mint heavy coins worth ten standard cash apiece, hoping to stabilize the skew between light and full-weight currency.

sentences.zh: 貞元初，駱谷、散關禁行人以一錢出者。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Zhenyuan, Luogu and San'guan passes forbade travelers to take out even a single coin.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Zhenyuan era, travelers at the Luogu and San'guan passes were barred from carrying so much as one coin beyond the frontier.

sentences.zh: 諸道鹽鐵使張滂奏禁江淮鑄銅為器，惟鑄鑑而已。

translations.literal: Circuit salt-and-iron commissioner Zhang Pang memorialized to forbid casting copper into vessels in the Jiang-Huai, permitting mirrors alone.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Pang, the salt-and-iron commissioner, urged a ban on copperware in the Jiang-Huai basin, allowing only the casting of mirrors.

sentences.zh: 十年，詔天下鑄銅器，每器一斤，其直不得過百六十，銷錢者以盜鑄論。

translations.literal: In the tenth year, an edict governed empire-wide casting of copper vessels: each vessel of one jin might not exceed one hundred sixty in price; those who melted coin were prosecuted as illicit minters.
translations.idiomatic: In year ten an edict regulated copperware empire-wide: no piece weighing one jin might sell for more than 160 cash, and anyone who melted coin to cast it would be treated as a counterfeiter.

sentences.zh: 然而民間錢益少，繒帛價輕，州縣禁錢不出境，商賈皆絕。

translations.literal: Yet popular coin grew ever scarcer, silk and cloth prices fell, prefectures and counties forbade coin to leave their borders, and merchants ceased altogether.
translations.idiomatic: All the same, cash in circulation dwindled, silk and cloth lost value, local governments blocked coin from crossing their borders, and trade ground to a halt.

sentences.zh: 浙西觀察使李若初請通錢往來，而京師商賈齎錢四方貿易者，不可勝計。

translations.literal: Zhexi surveillance commissioner Li Ruochu requested free circulation of coin, while capital merchants carrying coin to trade in all directions were beyond counting.
translations.idiomatic: Li Ruochu, commissioner of Zhexi, asked that coin be allowed to move freely again; meanwhile merchants in the capital were exporting cash in every direction in numbers too great to reckon.

sentences.zh: 詔復禁之。

translations.literal: An edict again forbade it.
translations.idiomatic: The throne ordered the restrictions reimposed.

sentences.zh: 二十年，命市井交易，以綾、羅、絹、布、雜貨與錢兼用。

translations.literal: In the twentieth year, market trade was ordered to use damask, gauze, silk, cloth, and miscellaneous goods together with coin.
translations.idiomatic: In year twenty the government required marketplace dealings to accept damask, gauze, silk, cloth, and other goods alongside cash.

sentences.zh: 憲宗以錢少復禁用銅器。

translations.literal: Emperor Xianzong, because coin was scarce, again forbade copper vessels.
translations.idiomatic: With the currency still too thin, Emperor Xianzong once more banned copper utensils.

sentences.zh: 時商賈至京師，委錢諸道進奏院及諸軍、諸使富家，以輕裝趨四方，合券乃取之，號「飛錢」。

translations.literal: At the time merchants arriving at the capital deposited coin with circuit memorial offices and the wealthy households of armies and commissioners, traveled light in all directions, and redeemed it only upon matching certificates—called "flying cash."
translations.idiomatic: Merchants bound for the capital would leave their coin with circuit memorial bureaus or with the treasuries of armies and commissioners, travel unburdened across the empire, and collect payment only when their vouchers matched—a practice known as "flying cash."

sentences.zh: 京兆尹裴武請禁與商賈飛錢者，廋索諸坊，十人為保。

translations.literal: Jingzhao governor Pei Wu requested a ban on flying cash with merchants, with thorough searches of the wards and groups of ten men as mutual guarantors.
translations.idiomatic: Pei Wu, governor of the capital district, urged a crackdown on flying-cash dealings with merchants, proposing ward-by-ward searches and mutual-responsibility groups of ten.

sentences.zh: 鹽鐵使李巽以郴州平陽銅坑二百八十餘，復置桂陽監，以兩鑪日鑄錢二十萬。

translations.literal: Salt-and-iron commissioner Li Xun, with more than 280 copper pits at Chenzhou's Pingyang, restored the Guiyang mint and, with two furnaces, cast 200,000 coins daily.
translations.idiomatic: Li Xun, commissioner of salt and iron, reopened the Guiyang mint to exploit more than 280 copper pits at Pingyang in Chenzhou, running two furnaces that turned out two hundred thousand coins a day.

sentences.zh: 天下歲鑄錢十三萬五千緡。

translations.literal: Empire-wide yearly coin casting came to 135,000 strings.
translations.idiomatic: Annual mint output across the realm reached 135,000 strings of cash.

sentences.zh: 命商賈蓄錢者，皆出以市貨；

translations.literal: Those merchants hoarding coin were ordered to release it for market goods;
translations.idiomatic: Merchants sitting on stockpiled cash were commanded to put it back into circulation by buying goods;

sentences.zh: 天下有銀之山必有銅，唯銀無益於人，五嶺以北，採銀一兩者流他州，官吏論罪。

translations.literal: Throughout the empire, wherever mountains held silver there was also copper; silver alone benefited no one—in lands north of the Five Ridges, anyone gathering even one liang of silver was exiled to another prefecture, and officials were punished by law.
translations.idiomatic: Wherever a mountain yielded silver it also held copper, but silver itself served no public need; north of the Five Ridges, even one liang of silver mined meant exile to another province, and complicit officials faced prosecution.

sentences.zh: 元和四年，京師用錢緡少二十及有鉛錫錢者，捕之；

translations.literal: In the fourth year of Yuanhe, in the capital those using strings short twenty per thousand or lead-and-tin coin were arrested;
translations.idiomatic: In Yuanhe 4 the capital authorities seized anyone paying with short-weight strings—twenty cash light per thousand—or with debased lead-and-tin coin;

sentences.zh: 非交易而錢行衢路者，不問。

translations.literal: Those not engaged in trade who carried coin on public roads were not questioned.
translations.idiomatic: People who simply carried cash on the street without conducting a transaction were left alone.

sentences.zh: 復詔采五嶺銀坑，禁錢出嶺。

translations.literal: An edict again ordered mining of silver pits in the Five Ridges and forbade coin to leave the region.
translations.idiomatic: The court also revived work in the Five Ridges' silver pits and barred cash from being taken beyond the mountains.

sentences.zh: 六年，貿易錢十緡以上者，參用布帛。

translations.literal: In the sixth year, trade involving ten strings of coin or more was to use cloth and silk in part.
translations.idiomatic: In year six, any transaction of ten strings or more had to include payment in cloth and silk as well as cash.

sentences.zh: 蔚州三河冶距飛狐故監二十里而近，河東節度使王鍔置鑪，疏拒馬河水鑄錢，工費尤省，以刺史李聽為使，以五鑪鑄，每鑪月鑄錢三十萬，自是河東錫錢皆廢。

translations.literal: Weizhou's Sanhe smeltery lay within twenty li of the old Feihu mint; Hedong military governor Wang E established furnaces there, diverted the Juma River to cast coin at especially low cost, appointed Prefect Li Ting as commissioner, and with five furnaces each cast 300,000 coins monthly; from then on tin coin in Hedong was entirely abolished.
translations.idiomatic: At Weizhou the Sanhe foundry stood barely twenty li from the former Feihu mint. Wang E, governor of Hedong, set up furnaces there, routed the Juma River to power them, and cut minting costs sharply. He put Prefect Li Ting in charge of five furnaces, each producing three hundred thousand coins a month—and from that point every debased tin coin in Hedong was withdrawn.

sentences.zh: 自京師禁飛錢，家有滯藏，物價寖輕。

translations.literal: From the time the capital forbade flying money, households had stagnant hoards, and commodity prices gradually grew light.
translations.idiomatic: Once the capital banned flying money, cash piled up in private hoards and prices slowly sank.

sentences.zh: 判度支盧坦、兵部尚書判戶部事王紹、鹽鐵使王播請許商人於戶部、度支、鹽鐵三司飛錢，每千錢增給百錢，然商人無至者。

translations.literal: Revenue Commissioner Lu Tan, Minister of War and concurrent Minister of Revenue Wang Shao, and Salt and Iron Commissioner Wang Bo requested permission for merchants to use flying money at the three offices of Revenue, the Revenue Bureau, and Salt and Iron, with an added grant of one hundred cash per thousand—but no merchants came.
translations.idiomatic: Revenue Commissioner Lu Tan, Minister of War Wang Shao in his concurrent post over the Ministry of Revenue, and Salt and Iron Commissioner Wang Bo petitioned to let merchants remit flying money through those three fiscal offices, offering a bonus of one hundred cash on every thousand—yet no merchant would use the scheme.

sentences.zh: 復許與商人敵貫而易之，然錢重帛輕如故。

translations.literal: They again permitted exchange with merchants at matching full strings, yet money remained heavy and silk cloth light as before.
translations.idiomatic: They again allowed merchants to swap coin at full nominal strings, but cash stayed scarce and cloth cheap as ever.

sentences.zh: 憲宗為之出內庫錢五十萬緡市布帛，每匹加舊估十之一。

translations.literal: Emperor Xianzong for this purpose released five hundred thousand strings from the inner treasury to buy cloth and silk, adding one-tenth to the old assessed price per bolt.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xianzong drew five hundred thousand strings from the palace treasury to buy up cloth and silk, paying one-tenth above the old official price per bolt.

sentences.zh: 會吳元濟、王承宗連衡拒命，以七道兵討之，經費屈竭。

translations.literal: It happened that Wu Yuanji and Wang Chengzong allied in defiance of orders; seven-route armies were sent to suppress them, and campaign funds were exhausted.
translations.idiomatic: Then Wu Yuanji and Wang Chengzong joined forces in open rebellion, and as seven military circuits marched against them, war funds ran dry.

sentences.zh: 皇甫鎛建議，內外用錢每緡墊二十外，復抽五十送度支以贍軍。

translations.literal: Huangfu Bo proposed that, beyond the twenty-cash shortfall per string already taken on money used at home and abroad, fifty cash more be skimmed from each string and sent to the Revenue Bureau to supply the army.
translations.idiomatic: Huangfu Bo proposed that on top of the usual twenty-cash short count per string, another fifty be withheld from every string spent inside or outside the capital and forwarded to the Revenue Bureau to feed the armies.

sentences.zh: 十二年，復給京兆府錢五十萬緡市布帛，而富家錢過五千貫者死，王公重貶，沒入於官，以五之一賞告者。

translations.literal: In the twelfth year, five hundred thousand strings were again granted to the Metropolitan Prefecture to buy cloth and silk; wealthy households with more than five thousand strings faced death, princes and nobles were heavily punished, property was confiscated by the state, and one-fifth was given to reward informants.
translations.idiomatic: In the twelfth year the court again gave the capital prefecture five hundred thousand strings to buy cloth and silk, while families hoarding more than five thousand strings were sentenced to death, princes and nobles were harshly penalized, their wealth was seized, and informants received a fifth of the confiscated sum.

sentences.zh: 京師區肆所積，皆方鎮錢，少亦五十萬緡，乃爭市第宅。

translations.literal: What accumulated in the capital's market stalls was all regional command money—none held less than five hundred thousand strings—and they competed to buy mansions.
translations.idiomatic: Cash piled up in the capital's shops was almost all money from the regional commands; even the smallest hoards ran to five hundred thousand strings, and merchants competed to buy grand houses.

sentences.zh: 然富賈倚左右神策軍官錢為名，府縣不敢劾問。

translations.literal: Yet wealthy merchants sheltered themselves under the name of official funds of the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies, and prefectural and county offices did not dare investigate or question them.
translations.idiomatic: Wealthy traders shielded their hoards by claiming them as official funds of the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies, and local officials did not dare probe them.

sentences.zh: 民間墊陌有至七十者，鉛錫錢益多，吏捕犯者，多屬諸軍、諸使，謼集市人彊奪，毆傷吏卒。

translations.literal: Among the people, short-shifting on the hundred-cash count reached as much as seventy; lead-tin coins grew ever more numerous. When officials arrested offenders, many belonged to various armies and commissioners; they called out market crowds to forcibly seize prisoners and beat and injure clerks and soldiers.
translations.idiomatic: Short counts in the marketplace ran as high as seventy cash per hundred, debased lead-and-tin coin proliferated, and when officers arrested violators—often men attached to armies or commissioner offices—their allies rallied market crowds to snatch the prisoners back and assault the arresting clerks and troops.

sentences.zh: 京兆尹崔元略請犯者本軍、本使涖決，帝不能用，詔送本軍、本使，而京兆府遣人涖決。

translations.literal: Metropolitan Prefect Cui Yuanlue requested that offenders be sent to their original army or commissioner for judgment on the spot; the emperor could not adopt this, and ordered offenders sent to their original army or commissioner while the Metropolitan Prefecture dispatched men to oversee the decision.
translations.idiomatic: Metropolitan Prefect Cui Yuanlue asked that offenders be returned to their own army or commissioner for trial, but the emperor would not agree; he ordered them sent back to those units while still requiring capital officials to be present at the hearing.

sentences.zh: 穆宗即位，京師鬻金銀十兩亦墊一兩，糴米鹽百錢墊七八。

translations.literal: When Emperor Muzong took the throne, in the capital the sale of ten taels of gold or silver also shorted one tael; buying rice or salt at one hundred cash shorted seven or eight.
translations.idiomatic: When Muzong came to the throne, even gold and silver trades in the capital shaved one tael off every ten, and a nominal hundred-cash purchase of rice or salt paid out only ninety-two or ninety-three.

sentences.zh: 京兆尹柳公綽以嚴法禁止之。

translations.literal: Metropolitan Prefect Liu Gongchuo forbade it by strict law.
translations.idiomatic: Metropolitan Prefect Liu Gongchuo cracked down on the practice with harsh penalties.

sentences.zh: 尋以所在用錢墊陌不一，詔從俗所宜，內外給用，每緡墊八十。

translations.literal: Soon, because short-shifting on money in use differed from place to place, an edict followed local custom as appropriate: for disbursements at home and abroad, eighty cash were shorted per string.
translations.idiomatic: Before long, with short counts varying from region to region, the court ruled that official payments at home and abroad should follow local practice—eighty cash short on every string.

sentences.zh: 寶曆初，河南尹王起請銷錢為佛像者以盜鑄錢論。

translations.literal: At the beginning of the Baoli era, Henan Prefect Wang Qi requested that those who melted coin to make Buddha images be prosecuted as illicit coin casters.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Baoli reign, Henan Prefect Wang Qi petitioned that anyone who melted coin into Buddha images be punished as an illicit minter.

sentences.zh: 大和三年，詔佛像以鉛、錫、土、木為之，飾帶以金銀、鍮石、烏油、藍鐵，唯鑑、磬、釘、鐶、鈕得用銅，餘皆禁之，盜鑄者死。

translations.literal: In the third year of Dahe, an edict ordered that Buddha images be made of lead, tin, earth, and wood; trim and bands might use gold, silver, brass, black iron, and blue iron; only mirrors, chime-stones, nails, rings, and buttons might use copper—all else was forbidden, and illicit casters were put to death.
translations.idiomatic: In Dahe 3 an edict required Buddha images to be cast from lead, tin, clay, or wood, with gold, silver, brass, black iron, or blue iron allowed only for ornament; copper was permitted solely for mirrors, chime-stones, nails, rings, and buttons. Everything else was banned, and illicit casting carried the death penalty.

sentences.zh: 是時峻鉛錫錢之禁，告千錢者賞以五千。

translations.literal: At this time the prohibition on lead-tin coin was made severe; one who reported a thousand cash received a reward of five thousand.
translations.idiomatic: The ban on debased lead-and-tin coin was enforced with special rigor, and informants who turned in a thousand cash of it were paid five thousand.

sentences.zh: 四年，詔積錢以七千緡為率，十萬緡者期以一年出之，二十萬以二年。

translations.literal: In the fourth year, an edict set seven thousand strings as the standard for hoarded money: holders of one hundred thousand strings had one year to spend it down, and two years for two hundred thousand.
translations.idiomatic: In the fourth year the court fixed seven thousand strings as the hoarding threshold: anyone sitting on one hundred thousand had to spend it within a year, and anyone with two hundred thousand within two.

sentences.zh: 凡交易百緡以上者，匹帛米粟居半。

translations.literal: For all transactions of one hundred strings or more, bolts of silk and rice or grain were to make up half.
translations.idiomatic: Any deal above one hundred strings had to be settled half in coin and half in cloth, rice, or grain.

sentences.zh: 河南府、揚州、江陵府以都會之劇，約束如京師。

translations.literal: Henan Prefecture, Yangzhou, and Jiangling Prefecture, because they were bustling metropolises, were placed under restrictions like those of the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Because Henan, Yangzhou, and Jiangling were major commercial hubs, they were subjected to the same coin controls as the capital.

sentences.zh: 未幾皆罷。

translations.literal: Before long all were abolished.
translations.idiomatic: The measures were soon dropped altogether.

sentences.zh: 八年，河東錫錢復起，鹽鐵使王涯置飛狐鑄錢院於蔚州，天下歲鑄錢不及十萬緡。

translations.literal: In the eighth year, pewter coin in Hedong rose again; Salt and Iron Commissioner Wang Ya established the Flying Fox Coin-Casting Office at Weizhou, and empire-wide yearly coin casting fell short of one hundred thousand strings.
translations.idiomatic: In the eighth year debased pewter coin reappeared in Hedong; Salt and Iron Commissioner Wang Ya opened a mint at Flying Fox in Weizhou, yet annual output empire-wide did not reach one hundred thousand strings.

sentences.zh: 文宗病幣輕錢重，詔方鎮縱錢穀交易。

translations.literal: Emperor Wenzong grieved that currency was light and money heavy, and ordered the regional commands to allow free exchange of money and grain.
translations.idiomatic: Distressed that goods were cheap while coin remained scarce, Emperor Wenzong ordered the regional commands to loosen restrictions on cash-and-grain trade.

sentences.zh: 時雖禁銅為器，而江淮、嶺南列肆鬻之，鑄千錢為器，售利數倍。

translations.literal: Although copper vessels were then forbidden, in the Jiang-Huai and Lingnan regions shops lined the streets selling them; casting one thousand cash into a vessel, the sale profit was several times over.
translations.idiomatic: Copper vessels were officially banned, yet shops in the Jiang-Huai and Lingnan regions sold them openly; melting a thousand cash into ware could fetch several times the metal's face value.

sentences.zh: 宰相李珏請加鑪鑄錢，於是禁銅器，官一切為市之。

translations.literal: Chief Minister Li Jue requested adding furnaces to cast coin; thereupon copper vessels were forbidden, and the government bought them all at market.
translations.idiomatic: Chief Minister Li Jue urged more mint furnaces; the court then outlawed copper ware and bought up every piece on the market.

sentences.zh: 天下銅坑五十，歲采銅二十六萬六千斤。

translations.literal: Under heaven there were fifty copper mines, yielding two hundred sixty-six thousand jin of copper yearly.
translations.idiomatic: Fifty copper mines operated across the empire, producing two hundred sixty-six thousand jin of copper each year.

sentences.zh: 及武宗廢浮屠法，永平監官李郁彥請以銅像、鍾、磬、鑪、鐸皆歸巡院，州縣銅益多矣。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wuzong abolished the Buddhist law, Yongping Directorate official Li Yuyan requested that copper images, bells, chime-stones, censers, and clappers all be turned over to the inspection commission; copper in prefectures and counties grew ever more abundant.
translations.idiomatic: After Wuzong suppressed Buddhism, Yongping Directorate officer Li Yuyan proposed that copper statues, bells, chime-stones, censers, and clappers be surrendered to the inspection commission, and copper supplies in the provinces swelled.

sentences.zh: 鹽鐵使以工有常力，不足以加鑄，許諸道觀察使皆得置錢坊。

translations.literal: The Salt and Iron Commissioner, because regular labor quotas were fixed and insufficient for added casting, permitted every circuit observation commissioner to establish coin workshops.
translations.idiomatic: The Salt and Iron Commissioner, finding fixed mint labor too limited for increased output, allowed every regional observation commissioner to open coin workshops.

sentences.zh: 淮南節度使李紳請天下以州名鑄錢，京師為京錢，大小徑寸，如開元通寶，交易禁用舊錢。

translations.literal: Huainan Military Governor Li Shen requested that under heaven coin be cast bearing prefecture names, with the capital's called Capital Coin, one inch in diameter like Kaiyuan tongbao; in trade old coin was forbidden.
translations.idiomatic: Huainan governor Li Shen proposed minting coins stamped with each prefecture's name—Capital Coin for the capital—sized one inch across like Kaiyuan tongbao, and outlawing older coin in commerce.

sentences.zh: 會宣宗即位，盡黜會昌之政，新錢以字可辨，復鑄為像。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xuanzong took the throne, he entirely dismissed the Huichang policies; the new coin could be told by its characters, and was melted again into images.
translations.idiomatic: When Xuanzong came to the throne he rolled back the Huichang reforms; the distinctive new coins were identified by their inscriptions and melted back into Buddhist images.

sentences.zh: 昭宗末，京師用錢八百五十為貫，每百纔八十五，河南府以八十為百云。

translations.literal: At the end of Emperor Zhaozong's reign, in the capital eight hundred fifty cash counted as one string, and only eighty-five made a hundred; Henan Prefecture, it is said, took eighty as one hundred.
translations.idiomatic: In the last years of Zhaozong's reign the capital counted only eight hundred fifty coins as a full string and paid out eighty-five per nominal hundred; Henan Prefecture, by report, treated eighty as a hundred.
